Personal injury protection medical expenses coverage level selected: $250,000 per person per accident. Signed by the named insured. Includes the required notice explaining the coverage choices.

Police report (Report):
Vehicle 2 failed to stop for a red signal on an icy road and struck vehicle 1 on the driver's side. Vehicle 2 driver cited. Vehicle 2 insured with another carrier; liability limits on file.
Damage: Spinal cord injury with long-term care needs. Pickup: driver's side crushed, total loss.
Third parties:
At-fault driver and his insurer
Policyholder's wife (family attendant care)
Evidence:
Signed PIP selection form
Police report with citation
Rehabilitation cost estimate
Medical records
What happened (answer): A genuine catastrophic injury caused by the other driver. His chosen PIP limit will be exhausted, and costs above it can be pursued from the at-fault driver.
Missing information (answer):
The at-fault driver's bodily injury liability limits
Whether the policyholder has health insurance or Medicare that pays after PIP
Innocent explanations (answer): Many policyholders chose lower PIP limits after the 2019 reforms on the strength of brief sales advice
Questions to ask (answer):
Ask for the at-fault driver's liability limits
Ask whether he has health insurance that will pay once PIP is exhausted
Next steps (answer):
Pay PIP medical benefits up to the $250,000 chosen, applying the Michigan fee schedules
Assess family-provided attendant care within the statutory weekly hour limit for family members
Explain plainly that allowable expenses above his PIP limit can be claimed from the at-fault driver, and refer him for legal advice
Handle the pickup under collision and note the mini-tort claim of up to $3,000 against the at-fault driver for vehicle damage he cannot otherwise recover
Review the sales file: if the choice was not properly explained, treat it as a complaint and escalate
Assessment (answer): Genuine, catastrophic and covered to the limit he chose. The large exposure above $250,000 sits with the at-fault driver, not this policy.
Recommended action (answer): Pay PIP to the limit, support the excess claim against the at-fault driver, and check how the PIP choice was sold.
Possible outcomes (answer):
PIP paid to the limit; excess medical claim settled with the at-fault driver’s insurer for its limits
Sales complaint upheld and goodwill paid
Tags: Michigan, no-fault, PIP choice, catastrophic injury, attendant care, mini-tort

Title: Limited tort, eight physical therapy sessions, and a demand for pain and suffering
Claim notification (exhibit A): Our policyholder rear-ended Ms Walsh's car at a light in Pittsburgh in the rain. Her attorney demands $60,000 for pain and suffering, saying she suffered a serious impairment of body function. Her own auto policy shows she chose the limited tort option. Her medical records show neck and back strain treated with eight physical therapy sessions, and she was back at her desk job two weeks after the crash.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): My neck and back were in agony for weeks. I still can't do my spin classes. Driving makes me anxious. I don't care what box I ticked on my insurance, I'm the one who got hurt and he hit me.
Other accounts:
Her auto policy declarations (Document):
Tort option: limited tort. Signed selection form on file. First-party medical benefits: $5,000.

Physical therapy discharge summary (Report):
Cervical and lumbar strain. Eight sessions over five weeks. Full range of motion restored. Discharged with a home exercise program. Returned to full-time work after two weeks.
Damage: Her Civic: rear bumper and trunk lid, $3,100, being paid. Injury: neck and back strain, resolved.
Third parties:
Megan Walsh
Her attorney
Evidence:
Her declarations page showing limited tort
Physical therapy discharge summary
Police report confirming our policyholder rear-ended her
What happened (answer): A genuine rear-end collision causing a soft-tissue injury that resolved in weeks. Under the limited tort option she cannot recover pain and suffering unless the injury is serious or an exception applies.
Missing information (answer): Any medical opinion that the injury is serious or permanent
Inconsistencies (answer): The demand describes a serious impairment; the treatment records show a full recovery in five weeks
Fraud indicators (answer): Pain and suffering demand by a limited tort claimant with a resolved soft-tissue injury
Innocent explanations (answer): Claimants often do not remember choosing limited tort when they bought the policy
Questions to ask (answer):
Ask the attorney which exception or which serious injury they rely on
Check whether any limited tort exception applies to our policyholder, such as a drunk-driving conviction
Next steps (answer):
Accept liability for the collision and pay her property damage
Decline the pain and suffering demand unless she shows a serious injury: limited tort bars non-economic damages otherwise
Consider economic losses above her own first-party benefits, which limited tort does not bar
Confirm no limited tort exception applies before closing the point
Assessment (answer): Genuine collision, real but minor injury, overstated demand. The limited tort election is decisive for pain and suffering unless a serious injury is shown.
Recommended action (answer): Pay the property damage and documented economic loss, decline non-economic damages, and invite medical evidence of a serious injury.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Demand withdrawn; small economic-loss settlement
Suit filed and dismissed on summary judgment under limited tort
Tags: Pennsylvania, limited tort, serious injury, non-economic damages, first-party benefits, soft tissue

Title: The roommate took the keys from the bowl
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder's roommate took her car keys from a bowl by the door while she was asleep in their Atlanta apartment and drove to a party. On the way back he hit a parked car and a fence. She says he never had permission to drive her car. Texts between them show she let him borrow it twice in the previous month. The owners of the parked car and the fence have both claimed against her policy.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): He asked me twice before and both times I said yes, but I was there and I knew where he was going. This time I was asleep and he just took it. I'd never have said yes at 1 in the morning when he'd been drinking. I don't want to get him in trouble but I'm not paying for this.
Other accounts:
Text messages between the policyholder and the roommate (Message or email):
Three weeks before: "can I borrow ur car for the store" "yes keys in the bowl". Ten days before: "need ur car for work tmrw?" "fine bring it back by 6". Night of the crash: no messages before 01:12, when he wrote "im so sorry i hit a car".

Roommate, Tyler Bishop (Statement):
She always said I could use it if I needed it, keys are in the bowl. I didn't wake her up because it was late. I'd had a couple of beers, I wasn't drunk. I feel terrible.
Damage: Parked Altima: rear quarter and bumper, $3,900. Fence: two panels, $1,100. Policyholder's car: front end, $4,300.
Third parties:
Tyler Bishop, roommate
Owner of the parked Altima
Owner of the fence
Evidence:
Text messages
Roommate's statement
Photos of the damage
Police report
What happened (answer): The roommate took the car without asking that night. Whether that was within an implied permission built up by earlier borrowing is the real question.
Missing information (answer):
Whether the roommate has his own auto policy
Whether alcohol testing was done
Inconsistencies (answer): She says he had no permission; he says she said he could use it whenever he needed
Innocent explanations (answer): Earlier permission with the keys left in a shared bowl can genuinely leave both sides with different understandings
Questions to ask (answer):
Ask whether she ever said he could use the car without asking each time
Ask whether the roommate has his own insurance
Next steps (answer):
Investigate permission: express permission, any pattern of implied permission, and whether this use went beyond it
If permission is found, the policy’s liability cover extends to him as a permissive user; if not, the third parties’ claims fall to his own cover or to them
Check his own auto policy, which may respond either way
Handle her own car under collision if cover applies and explain the decision
Assessment (answer): Genuinely disputed. The prior borrowing and the shared key bowl support implied permission, but taking the car at night without asking, after drinking, may fall outside it.
Recommended action (answer): Take statements, check his own insurance, and make a reasoned permissive-use decision.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Implied permission found; third parties paid under her policy
Use found to exceed any permission; third parties referred to his own insurer
Tags: Georgia, permissive use, implied permission, roommate, liability coverage, text messages

Title: A Tacoma valued with comparables 300 miles away
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder's 2019 Toyota Tacoma was declared a total loss after a rear-end collision in Phoenix. The insurer's valuation report put its actual cash value at $31,200, using comparables from dealers up to 300 miles away and a "rough" interior condition rating. He sent four local dealer listings for similar trucks priced between $35,900 and $37,400 and a photo of the interior, and has invoked the policy's appraisal clause in writing.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): The interior was spotless, I've got photos from the week before. Their comparables are from Tucson and Flagstaff, not Phoenix, and two of them were base models. Trucks like mine sell here in days. I don't want a fight, I just want what it's worth.
Other accounts:
Valuation report extract (Report):
Base value $33,050 from five comparable vehicles within 300 miles. Condition adjustment: interior rough, minus $1,850. Final actual cash value $31,200. Two comparables are SR trims without the off-road package.

Policy appraisal clause (Document):
If we and you do not agree on the amount of loss, either may demand an appraisal. Each party selects an appraiser; the two appraisers select an umpire. A decision agreed by any two is binding on the amount of loss.
Damage: Tacoma TRD Off-Road: rear frame and bed damage, total loss.
Third parties: The at-fault driver who rear-ended him and their insurer
Evidence:
Valuation report
Local dealer listings
Owner's interior photos
Appraisal demand letter
What happened (answer): A genuine total loss where the valuation understated the truck's value through distant, lower-spec comparables and an unsupported condition deduction.
Missing information (answer): The inspector’s notes or photos supporting the rough interior rating
Inconsistencies (answer): The report rates the interior rough; his recent photos show it clean
Innocent explanations (answer): Valuation tools often widen the search radius when local stock is thin
Questions to ask (answer): Ask the inspector for the photos behind the condition rating
Next steps (answer):
Re-run the valuation with local comparables of the same trim and remove the condition deduction unless it is supported
If agreement is still not reached, appoint the insurer’s appraiser within the policy time limit and cooperate with the umpire process
Pay the undisputed amount now rather than holding everything back
Recover the payout from the at-fault driver’s insurer
Assessment (answer): Genuine claim with a fair valuation complaint. The appraisal clause is his right; correcting the report may settle it without one.
Recommended action (answer): Revalue with like-for-like local comparables, pay the undisputed sum, and take part in the appraisal if needed.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Revalued at $35,800 and accepted; appraisal withdrawn
Appraisal panel sets $36,200
Tags: Arizona, actual cash value, valuation report, comparables, appraisal clause, umpire

Title: Aftermarket headlamps in front of the radar
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder's one-year-old Honda CR-V hit a concrete parking barrier in the rain in Chicago. The insurer's estimate uses aftermarket parts for the bumper cover, the headlamps and the grille emblem. The repairer says the manufacturer's repair procedures call for original parts where they affect the radar and camera systems, and that an aftermarket grille emblem may stop the radar working. She wants original parts throughout.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): It's a year old with 10,000 miles. The adaptive cruise and the emergency braking are why I bought it. The body shop says cheap parts could make the radar unreliable. I don't want to find out on the highway. Surely you have to put it back the way Honda built it?
Other accounts:
Repairer’s note (Report):
Manufacturer position statement: radar-transparent grille emblem must be genuine; non-genuine emblems may cause radar misreads. Headlamps with adaptive lighting require calibration with genuine units. Bumper cover: certified aftermarket acceptable if sensor brackets are genuine. Calibration of radar and camera required after repair.

Insurer’s estimate summary (Document):
Aftermarket bumper cover, headlamps (pair) and grille emblem. Calibration not included. Total $3,950.
Damage: CR-V: bumper cover, grille emblem, both headlamps, radar bracket. No structural damage.
Third parties: None
Evidence:
Repairer's note citing the manufacturer position statement
Insurer's estimate
Photos of the damage
What happened (answer): A genuine low-speed impact. The estimate used aftermarket parts on safety-related components where the manufacturer requires genuine parts, and left out calibration.
Missing information (answer): The parts disclosure the estimate should have given her
Innocent explanations (answer): Estimating systems default to aftermarket parts unless the assessor overrides them
Questions to ask (answer): Ask the repairer for the manufacturer position statement document
Next steps (answer):
Specify genuine parts for the radar-transparent emblem, the sensor bracket and the adaptive headlamps, as the manufacturer requires
Add radar and camera calibration to the estimate
Allow a certified aftermarket bumper cover only if the repairer confirms it does not affect the sensors, and disclose any non-original parts to her in writing as Illinois requires
Fix the estimating rule for ADAS-related parts on newer vehicles
Assessment (answer): Genuine claim and a reasonable objection. Safety systems are the deciding factor: parts in the radar and camera path should be genuine, with calibration.
Recommended action (answer): Revise the estimate to genuine safety-related parts plus calibration, and disclose any remaining aftermarket parts.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Revised estimate $5,480 with calibration; repair completed
Customer complaint closed with the revised estimate
Tags: OEM parts, aftermarket parts, ADAS, radar, repair procedures, calibration

Title: A total loss offer with no sales tax, and a lift kit with no receipts
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder's 2020 Ford F-150 was a total loss after a head-on collision on a rural road near Fresno. The insurer offered $34,000 less her $500 deductible. The offer does not include sales tax or the license and transfer fees for a comparable vehicle. She has also claimed $8,000 for aftermarket upgrades: a lift kit, wheels and a light bar. She has no receipts, and the photos on file show the wheels and light bar but a standard ride height.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): My husband did the upgrades himself, he paid cash at swap meets so there are no receipts. The wheels alone were $2,500. Everyone else I know got their sales tax back on a total loss. Why didn't I?
Other accounts:
Settlement offer letter (Document):
Actual cash value $34,000, less deductible $500. Total $33,500. Tax and fees: not included.

Policy, custom equipment (Document):
Custom parts or equipment are covered up to $1,500 unless scheduled on the policy for a higher amount. No custom equipment scheduled.
Damage: F-150: front end and frame, total loss. Aftermarket wheels and light bar fitted; no lift kit visible in photos.
Third parties: The other driver and their insurer
Evidence:
Settlement offer letter
Custom equipment clause
Photos of the truck before and after the crash
What happened (answer): A genuine total loss. The insurer's offer left out tax and fees that California requires, and the claim for upgrades is partly unsupported: the truck was never lifted.
Missing information (answer):
Any proof of the cost of the wheels and light bar
A photo showing a lift kit
Inconsistencies (answer): She claims a lift kit; the photos show a standard ride height
Fraud indicators (answer): Undocumented upgrades claimed at a round figure
Innocent explanations (answer):
Cash purchases at swap meets genuinely leave no receipts
She may be repeating what her husband told her
Questions to ask (answer):
Ask for any photos, bank records or listings for the wheels and the light bar
Ask whether the lift kit was fitted or only bought
Next steps (answer):
Add sales tax and the license, registration and transfer fees for a comparable vehicle, as California’s fair claims regulations require for a total loss settlement
Pay the wheels and light bar within the $1,500 custom equipment limit, on reasonable evidence of value
Decline the lift kit unless there is evidence it was fitted
Explain the revised figure in writing
Assessment (answer): Genuine total loss with two separate problems: the insurer underpaid by leaving out tax and fees, and the claimant overstated the upgrades.
Recommended action (answer): Reissue the offer with tax and fees, pay custom equipment up to the limit, and decline the unproven lift kit.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Revised settlement paid with tax and fees plus $1,500 for equipment
Department of Insurance complaint closed after the revised offer
Tags: California, total loss, sales tax, registration fees, custom equipment, Fair Claims Settlement Practices

Title: Totaled by the numbers, but he wants to keep his Civic

Total loss evaluation (Report):
Repair estimate $9,800. Actual cash value $9,200. Salvage bid $1,700. Repair exceeds value: total loss. Owner requests to retain the vehicle.

Police report (Report):
Vehicle 2 failed to control speed in heavy rain and struck vehicle 1 from behind. Vehicle 2 driver cited. Vehicle 2 insured.
Damage: Civic: rear bumper, trunk, rear panel and both rear quarter panels. Drivable.
Third parties: The driver who rear-ended him and their insurer
Evidence:
Total loss evaluation
Police report
Photos

Missing information (answer): Confirmation there is no lienholder on the title
Innocent explanations (answer): Older cars often become total losses on cost even when they still drive
Questions to ask (answer): Confirm whether there is a loan on the car

Agree the owner-retained settlement: actual cash value less the salvage value and the deductible
Follow Texas rules for owner-retained total losses: report it so the title is branded salvage, and explain that the car needs a rebuilt title and inspection before it can be registered again
Recover the payment and his deductible from the at-fault driver’s insurer
Explain the effect of a branded title on the car’s future value
Assessment (answer): Genuine and straightforward. He can keep the car with the salvage value deducted, provided the title is handled correctly.
Recommended action (answer): Pay the owner-retained settlement, complete the salvage title steps, and pursue subrogation.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Paid $7,000 after salvage and deductible; deductible later reimbursed through subrogation

Title: A new knee for a knee that was already due for one
Claim notification (exhibit A): Our policyholder rear-ended Mr Jensen, aged 72, at a light in Tucson. He claims the crash injured his right knee and caused the need for a knee replacement, which Medicare paid for. His records show osteoarthritis in that knee and a surgeon's note recommending replacement eight months before the crash. Medicare has paid $18,400 for treatment since the accident. His attorney demands the policy limit of $100,000.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): My knee hit the dashboard hard. Before the accident I was managing, I played golf twice a week. Afterwards I couldn't walk without a cane. The surgeon said it had to be done. I'm not trying to get anything I don't deserve.
Other accounts:
Orthopedic note, eight months before the crash (Report):
Severe osteoarthritis of the right knee, bone on bone medially. Discussed total knee replacement; patient wishes to delay. Continue injections and a cane as needed.

Medicare conditional payment summary (Record or log):
Conditional payments related to the accident date: $18,400, including the knee replacement. Final demand to be issued once the settlement is reported.
Damage: Knee contusion with aggravation of existing osteoarthritis; knee replacement. Car: rear bumper and trunk.
Third parties:
Harold Jensen
His attorney
Medicare
Evidence:
Pre-accident orthopedic note
Medicare conditional payment summary
Post-accident medical records
Police report
What happened (answer): A genuine collision that probably aggravated a knee that already needed replacing. The claim treats the whole surgery as caused by the crash.
Missing information (answer):
An independent orthopedic opinion on how far the crash advanced the surgery
Golf club or activity records before and after the crash
Inconsistencies (answer): He says he was managing well before the crash; his surgeon recommended a replacement eight months earlier
Fraud indicators (answer): Claiming a planned surgery as wholly caused by the accident
Innocent explanations (answer): A collision can genuinely bring forward an operation that someone was putting off
Questions to ask (answer): Ask the attorney for all records for the knee in the five years before the crash
Next steps (answer):
Value the claim as an aggravation: the crash may have brought the surgery forward, but it did not cause the arthritis
Get an independent orthopedic opinion on the acceleration
Because he is a Medicare beneficiary, report the settlement under Section 111 and resolve Medicare’s conditional payment claim before or at settlement, so Medicare is reimbursed
Make sure the settlement terms deal with Medicare’s interest
Assessment (answer): Genuine accident, real aggravation, overstated causation. The Medicare obligations are mandatory whatever the amount agreed.
Recommended action (answer): Value as an aggravation with an independent opinion, and build Medicare reporting and reimbursement into the settlement.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Settled at $42,000 with Medicare reimbursed from the settlement
Mediation agrees $55,000 after the independent opinion
Tags: Medicare, Section 111 reporting, conditional payments, pre-existing condition, aggravation, knee replacement

Title: A food truck off the road for six weeks, and the profits it says it lost
Claim notification (exhibit A): Our policyholder backed out of a space in Austin and hit a parked food truck, damaging its side and serving window. Liability is accepted. The truck's owner claims $6,800 for repairs and $24,000 for six weeks of lost profits while it was off the road. The body shop's records show the repair took 9 working days, after the owner waited three weeks before authorizing it.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): That truck is my whole business. We do lunch at the tech campuses and a brewery every weekend. I had to cancel two festival bookings. I waited to authorize the repair because your adjuster hadn't confirmed you'd pay, and I couldn't afford to front $6,800.
Other accounts:
Body shop record (Record or log):
Vehicle dropped off 2 days after the collision. Estimate sent to the owner the same day. Authorization received 23 days later. Repair completed in 9 working days.

Adjuster’s file note (Record or log):
Liability accepted on day 4. Owner asked whether we would pay the shop directly. Callback promised; next contact recorded on day 22.
Damage: Food truck: nearside panels and serving window, $6,800. Lost trading for about six weeks.
Third parties: Rosalind Pierce, owner of the food truck
Evidence:
Body shop record
Adjuster's file note
Repair invoice
What happened (answer): A genuine claim for a working vehicle. Some of the time off the road was caused by the insurer's own slow response, so the delay cannot all be blamed on the owner.
Missing information (answer):
Tax returns or sales records for the same weeks in earlier years
The cancelled festival booking contracts
Fraud indicators (answer): Lost profits claimed at a round figure without records
Innocent explanations (answer): Small businesses often cannot fund repairs before the insurer confirms payment
Questions to ask (answer):
Ask for sales records and tax returns to calculate net lost profit
Ask for the festival booking confirmations and cancellations
Next steps (answer):
Pay the repair cost
Assess loss of use as net lost profit, not gross sales, supported by records
Include the period caused by the insurer’s own delay in confirming payment; the owner’s duty to mitigate does not cover delay the insurer caused
Pay the documented amount promptly and explain the calculation
Assessment (answer): Genuine and recoverable in principle. The amount needs records, and the insurer's own 18-day silence weakens any mitigation argument.
Recommended action (answer): Pay the repairs, request sales records, and pay net lost profit for the whole period the insurer's delay caused.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Net lost profit of $14,900 paid on the sales records
Owner files a complaint about the callback delay; upheld

Title: A policy-limits demand with 30 days to run, and 22 already gone
Claim notification (exhibit A): Our policyholder ran a red light in Atlanta and struck Ms Carter's car; she suffered a fractured femur. His bodily injury limit is $50,000 per person. Her medical bills already exceed $92,000. Her attorney sent a time-limited demand to settle for the $50,000 limit, open for 30 days, with conditions on payment timing and a sworn statement of any other insurance. Twenty-two days have passed. The adjuster has asked for medical records that were already enclosed.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): He told me he looked away for a second. I was in surgery twice and I still can't walk properly. My lawyer says the other side has thirty days and they're wasting them.
Other accounts:
Demand letter (summary) (Document):
Offer to settle all claims against your insured for the $50,000 bodily injury limit. Acceptance must be in writing within 30 days of receipt. Payment within 10 days of acceptance. Provide a sworn statement of all other insurance available to your insured. Medical records and bills totalling $92,416 enclosed.

Police report (Report):
Vehicle 1 entered the intersection against a steady red signal and struck vehicle 2. Vehicle 1 driver cited for failing to obey a traffic control device. Two independent witnesses.
Damage: Fractured femur, two surgeries, medical bills $92,416 so far. Her car: total loss.
Third parties:
Denise Carter
Her attorney
Evidence:
Time-limited demand with enclosures
Police report with citation and witnesses
Medical bills
What happened (answer): Clear liability and damages far above the limit. The insurer is close to letting a reasonable demand within limits expire.
Missing information (answer): Confirmation of any other insurance covering the policyholder, such as an umbrella policy
Innocent explanations (answer): The adjuster may not have realised that the demand carries a strict deadline and conditions
Questions to ask (answer): Ask the policyholder at once whether he has an umbrella or any other policy that might apply
Next steps (answer):
Escalate today to a senior handler and coverage or defense counsel
Calculate the exact deadline from the date of receipt and diarize it
Accept the demand in writing within the time limit if, as it appears, liability is clear and damages exceed the limit, and meet every condition exactly, including the sworn statement and payment timing
Tell the policyholder in writing about the demand and his personal exposure above the limit
Do not ask again for records already provided; record the reasons for the decision
Assessment (answer): Genuine, clear liability, damages well above limits. Letting this demand lapse would expose the insurer to a bad faith claim for the full excess judgment.
Recommended action (answer): Accept the policy-limits demand within the deadline and comply with all its conditions.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Demand accepted on day 27; settled for the limit
Missed deadline leads to a $410,000 verdict and a bad faith claim

Title: Turning left in Orlando, hit by a driver doing 58 and texting
Claim notification (exhibit A): Our policyholder turned left at a green light in Orlando and was struck by Ms Nguyen's oncoming car. She has sued him for her injuries, saying he failed to yield. The accident happened in 2025. Her car's event data recorder shows 58 mph five seconds before impact in a 40 mph zone. Her phone records, obtained in discovery, show a text sent 4 seconds before the crash.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): I had a green light. He turned right in front of me, there was nothing I could do. Yes, I was going a bit fast, everyone does on that road. I wasn't texting, I might have sent a voice message.
Other accounts:
Event data recorder download (claimant’s car) (Record or log):
Speed 58 mph at 5.0 seconds before the event, 57 mph at 1.0 second, brake applied 0.6 seconds before the event. Posted limit 40 mph.

Our policyholder (Statement):
I waited for a gap. Her car was far enough away when I started to turn, it just arrived much faster than I expected. I never saw her brake.
Damage: Claimant: fractured wrist and facial injuries. Both cars: total losses.
Third parties:
Tara Nguyen
Her attorneys
Evidence:
Event data recorder download
Phone records showing a text 4 seconds before impact
Policyholder's statement
Police report
What happened (answer): A left-turn collision where the turning driver had a duty to yield, but the oncoming driver was 18 mph over the limit and probably using her phone. Fault may well be more than half hers.
Missing information (answer):
An accident reconstruction of whether the turn was safe at the legal speed
Witness accounts
Inconsistencies (answer): She says she was not texting; her phone records show a text sent 4 seconds before impact
Innocent explanations (answer): Voice-to-text can register as a sent text
Questions to ask (answer): Commission a reconstruction: would she have stopped or passed safely at 40 mph?
Next steps (answer):
Apply Florida’s modified comparative negligence rule for accidents after 24 March 2023: a claimant more than 50% at fault recovers nothing
Build the fault case with the event data, the phone records and a reconstruction
Value the case on a realistic apportionment and consider a proposal for settlement if exposure remains
Check the claim was filed within Florida’s two-year limitation period for negligence
Assessment (answer): Disputed liability with strong evidence against the claimant. If she is found more than 50% at fault, the 2023 rule bars her claim entirely.
Recommended action (answer): Defend on comparative fault with reconstruction evidence, and settle only at a figure that reflects the risk.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Jury finds her 60% at fault; no recovery
Settled at a modest figure before trial

Title: A flashing red, two drivers who both stopped first, and a 70/30 award
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder collided with another car at a Denver intersection where the signals were flashing red in all directions after a snowstorm. Each driver says they stopped first. Her collision claim was paid at $7,400 less her $1,000 deductible. The insurer filed for inter-company arbitration seeking 100% from the other insurer, which answered 50/50. The arbitrator awarded 70/30 in her favour. She has asked when she gets her deductible back.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): I stopped, looked both ways and went. He came from the right without stopping, I'm sure of it. I've paid my deductible and I've been told I might get it back. When?
Other accounts:
Arbitration decision (Document):
Flashing red signals operate as an all-way stop. Witness evidence favours the applicant's insured as first to arrive; respondent's insured likely failed to stop fully. Liability: respondent 70%, applicant 30%.

Witness at the bus stop (Witness account):
The blue car stopped and pulled out. The silver car slowed down but I don't think it stopped, it kind of rolled through.
Damage: Her Subaru: front-left corner, $8,400 total including the deductible. Other car: right front.
Third parties: The other driver and their insurer
Evidence:
Arbitration decision
Bus stop witness's statement
Payment record
What happened (answer): A genuine intersection collision with shared fault. The arbitration award recovers 70% of the payment, and the policyholder is owed a share of it for her deductible.
Missing information (answer): Traffic signal maintenance log confirming the flashing mode
Inconsistencies (answer): Each driver says they stopped first
Innocent explanations (answer): After a storm, drivers often misjudge who arrived first at an all-way stop
Questions to ask (answer): Confirm what the policy and Colorado law say about sharing recoveries with the insured
Next steps (answer):
Collect 70% of the $8,400 loss from the other insurer under the award
Reimburse her deductible from the recovery as the policy and Colorado law require, at least in proportion to the recovery
Tell her the outcome and the amount refunded, and explain the 30% that stays with her
Close the file only once the recovery is received
Assessment (answer): Genuinely disputed liability, resolved fairly by arbitration. The remaining task is to pass on her share of the recovery promptly.
Recommended action (answer): Collect the 70% and refund her deductible share without delay.
Possible outcomes (answer):
$5,880 recovered; $700 of her deductible refunded
Full deductible refunded under the made-whole rule

Title: The tread came off the rear tire on the I-40
Accident type: Single vehicle or loss of control
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder's SUV rolled over on the I-40 near Amarillo when the tread came off the left rear tire at highway speed. She and her son had minor injuries. Claimant's statement (exhibit B): There was a bang and the back end swung round, then we rolled. The tires were nearly new, I keep the receipts for everything, they rotated them in the spring. I thought tires just didn't do that anymore.
Other accounts:
Tire service records (Record or log):
Four tires fitted 23 months before the crash. Rotations and pressure checks at 7,400, 15,100 and 22,800 miles; all pressures within specification; no damage noted.

Trooper’s report (Report):
Left rear tire tread separated; tread found on the shoulder 200 feet before the rollover. No signs of speeding. Weather hot and dry.
Damage: SUV total loss, $38,000. Minor injuries to the driver and her son.
Third parties:
Tire manufacturer
Tire retailer
Evidence:
Tire service records
Trooper's report
The tire and the separated tread at the tow yard
Photos of the scene
What happened (answer): A rollover caused by a tread separation on a properly maintained, nearly new tire, pointing to a possible manufacturing defect.
Missing information (answer):
A tire expert's examination
The tire identification number and any recall check

Stop the salvage sale and preserve the vehicle, the tire, the wheel and the separated tread with a documented chain of custody
Check the tire identification number against recalls
Instruct a tire expert, and notify the manufacturer and retailer so they can attend a joint inspection, avoiding any spoliation argument
Pay her total loss and injury benefits now; pursue subrogation for the total loss and benefits paid if a defect is found

Title: A rental payment to a vendor nobody had heard of
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder complained that she never received the $1,260 rental reimbursement promised after her car was rear-ended in Denver. The payment system shows it was paid to "Mile High Auto Rentals". That vendor was set up four months ago by the adjuster who handled her claim. Claimant's statement (exhibit B): I paid for the rental myself with my credit card and sent you the receipt from the real rental company. The adjuster said the check was in the mail. That was eight weeks ago. Now nobody calls me back.
Other accounts:
Vendor master record (Record or log):
Vendor: Mile High Auto Rentals. Created by user ID of the handling adjuster. Tax ID not verified. Address: a mailbox store. Bank account added the same day. 23 payments totalling $31,870 on 19 claims, all assigned to the same adjuster.

Rental company receipt (Document):
Rental paid by the policyholder's card: 14 days, $1,260. Rental company is a national chain, not Mile High Auto Rentals.
Damage: Customer unpaid $1,260. Possible insider loss of $31,870 across 19 claims.
Third parties:
The handling adjuster
Other affected customers
Evidence:
Vendor master record
Customer's rental receipt
Payment history for the vendor account
What happened (answer): The customer's claim is genuine. Her reimbursement was diverted to a fictitious vendor controlled by the adjuster, who appears to have done the same on other claims.
Missing information (answer):
Bank records for the vendor account
Whether other customers on the 19 claims were paid
Inconsistencies (answer): Payment recorded to a rental company she never used
Fraud indicators (answer):
Vendor created by the same person who approves its payments
Unverified tax ID and a mailbox address
Payments concentrated on one adjuster’s claims
Innocent explanations (answer): Data entry errors can misdirect a single payment, but not 23 payments to an unverified vendor
Questions to ask (answer): Check every one of the 19 claims for customers who were not paid
Next steps (answer):
Pay the customer her $1,260 now and apologize: she is not part of the problem
Refer to the special investigations unit and internal audit, preserve the system records, and restrict the adjuster’s access pending investigation
Contact every customer on the affected claims and pay anyone who was not paid
Fix the control gap: no user should be able to create a vendor and approve payments to it
Report as required to the state fraud bureau and law enforcement
Assessment (answer): The claim is genuine; the fraud is internal. The priority is to make the customer whole, then contain and investigate the insider scheme.
Recommended action (answer): Pay the customer, escalate to investigations and audit, and close the control gap.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Adjuster dismissed and charged; all affected customers paid
Vendor controls changed to require independent approval

Title: Stolen from the mall on the 12th, on a ship since the 25th of last month
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder reported his 2022 Lexus RX stolen from a mall parking lot in Newark, New Jersey, on 12 September. He produced both keys. A routine export check of the VIN shows the vehicle was declared for export and loaded into a container at Port Newark on 25 August, eighteen days before the reported theft. The vehicle is financed and he made his 1 September loan payment.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): I parked by the food court and went in for an hour. When I came out it was gone. I've got both keys right here. I don't know anything about any export, maybe someone cloned my VIN. I need the money to pay off the loan.
Other accounts:
Export record check (Record or log):
VIN matches a used vehicle export declaration filed 22 August. Container loaded at Port Newark on 25 August. Exporter: a freight forwarder in Elizabeth, NJ. Title copy submitted with the declaration in the policyholder's name.

Mall security (Record or log):
No camera coverage of the stated parking row. Entrance camera footage for 12 September reviewed for the plate: no match found entering the lot.
Damage: Claimed total loss $52,000. No damage; vehicle overseas.
Third parties:
Freight forwarder
Finance company
Evidence:
Export record with title copy
Mall camera review
Theft report
Both keys
What happened (answer): The car was exported with a copy of his title before he reported it stolen. The theft report is false.
Missing information (answer): The freight forwarder’s booking records and who paid them
Inconsistencies (answer):
Reported stolen on 12 September; exported on 25 August
Entrance cameras show no sign of the car entering the lot
Fraud indicators (answer):
Export with his title copy before the reported theft
Both keys produced
Financed vehicle
Innocent explanations (answer): VIN cloning exists, but a declaration with his own title copy makes it very unlikely
Questions to ask (answer):
Ask the freight forwarder who booked and paid for the export
Ask the policyholder to explain how a copy of his title was used
Next steps (answer):
Refer to the special investigations unit and to the National Insurance Crime Bureau
Get the freight forwarder’s records through the proper legal process
Take an examination under oath under the policy if the facts are disputed
Deny the claim on the evidence and report to the state fraud bureau as required
Assessment (answer): Confirmed fraud: the car was exported with his title copy 18 days before he reported it stolen.
Recommended action (answer): Deny, refer to the special investigations unit and NICB, and report to the state.

Claim withdrawn after the forwarder names him as the customer; prosecuted
Denied after the examination under oath

Title: Fifty-two days and no decision, in California
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder reported a collision claim on 2 June after her car was sideswiped in a San Jose parking structure. She sent photos, the repair estimate and the other driver's details on 10 June. The adjuster went on leave. Nobody acknowledged the claim until 21 June, and on 1 August, 52 days after her proof of claim, there is still no decision and no letter explaining what is needed. She has filed a complaint with the Department of Insurance.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): I sent everything you asked for in the first week. I've called nine times and left messages. Nobody told me anything was missing. I'm paying for a rental out of my own pocket. I've complained to the state because I didn't know what else to do.
Other accounts:
Claim activity log (Record or log):
2 June: first notice. 10 June: proof of claim received (estimate, photos, other party details). 21 June: acknowledgment sent. No further written communication. Nine inbound calls logged, no return calls. Adjuster on leave from 8 June; file not reassigned.

Department of Insurance complaint notice (Document):
Consumer complaint received regarding delay in claim handling. Please provide a full response and copies of all correspondence.
Damage: Her Corolla: driver's side doors, estimate $2,950. Rental costs paid by her.
Third parties: The other driver and their insurer
Evidence:
Claim activity log
Department of Insurance complaint notice
Her estimate and photos
What happened (answer): A straightforward claim left unattended when the adjuster went on leave, breaching California's time limits for acknowledging, deciding and communicating.
Missing information (answer): Any reason the file was not reassigned during the leave
Innocent explanations (answer): An unplanned leave without a handover can leave a file invisible to the rest of the team
Questions to ask (answer): Check whether other files of the same adjuster were left unassigned
Next steps (answer):
Decide the claim now and pay within the time allowed after acceptance
Recognise the breaches: acknowledgment is due within 15 calendar days of notice, and acceptance or denial within 40 days of proof of claim, with written notice every 30 days if more time is needed
Respond fully and promptly to the Department of Insurance with the file history
Reimburse her reasonable rental costs caused by the delay and apologize
Reassign the adjuster’s other files and fix the leave cover process
Assessment (answer): Genuine claim, clear regulatory breaches by the insurer. The fix is to pay, answer the regulator candidly and stop it recurring.
Recommended action (answer): Pay the claim and rental costs, respond to the Department of Insurance, and review the leave cover process.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Claim paid in 3 days; complaint closed with a finding against the insurer
Audit finds 14 other files of the same adjuster overdue
Tags: California, Fair Claims Settlement Practices Regulations, 15 days, 40 days, written status letter, Department of Insurance

Title: The claim file that went to the other Michael Brown
Claim notification (exhibit A): An adjuster in Boston emailed the injury claim file of policyholder Michael J. Brown to a different claimant, Michael R. Brown, because the email address auto-completed. The attachment included his driver's license image, medical records and a medical bill showing his Social Security number. The recipient replied an hour later: "I think this isn't mine." The adjuster has not told anyone.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): I was rear-ended in March and I've been through enough. Now you're telling me a stranger has my medical records and my Social Security number? What are you going to do about it?
Other accounts:
Email record (Record or log):
Sent 14:06 to michael.r.brown@ (another claimant's address) instead of michael.j.brown@. Attachment: claim file PDF, 41 pages, not encrypted. Reply received 15:02: "I think this isn't mine, I haven't opened most of it."

Attachment contents (Document):
Driver's license image; hospital and physical therapy records; a medical bill showing the full Social Security number; claim notes.
Damage: Exposure of driver's license, medical records and Social Security number. No financial loss known yet.
Third parties: Michael R. Brown, the unintended recipient
Evidence:
Email record
Attachment contents
Recipient's reply
What happened (answer): A genuine claim, and a privacy incident caused by an auto-completed email address. Sensitive personal information went to an unintended recipient.
Missing information (answer): Written confirmation from the recipient that the email and attachment are deleted
Innocent explanations (answer): Auto-complete errors are a common cause of misdirected email
Questions to ask (answer): Ask the recipient to confirm in writing that he has deleted the email and any copies
Next steps (answer):
Report the incident to the privacy or compliance team today, as company policy requires
Contain it: ask the recipient to delete the email and confirm in writing
Assess notification duties under the state breach notification and insurance data security laws: a Social Security number and medical records are sensitive data
Notify the policyholder, offer credit monitoring, and notify regulators if the law requires
Fix the cause: send sensitive files only through a secure portal, and turn off auto-complete for external addresses
Assessment (answer): The injury claim is genuine; the incident is the insurer's. Sensitive data was exposed, so containment, assessment and likely notification are needed promptly.
Recommended action (answer): Escalate to the privacy team, contain the disclosure, notify the policyholder with support, and assess regulatory notification.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Recipient confirms deletion; policyholder notified with credit monitoring; regulator notified
Secure portal made mandatory for medical records

Title: A recorded statement in English, and a customer who speaks Spanish
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder, whose first language is Spanish, gave a recorded statement in English two days after a collision at a stop sign in San Antonio. In it she answers "yes" to the question "So you didn't stop at the sign?" The adjuster assigned her 100% fault. Her daughter has called to say her mother did not understand the questions and did stop. A neighbour's doorbell camera has since been found.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): (Through her daughter, translated) I stopped at the sign. I always stop there, my grandchildren's school is on that street. The man on the phone talked very fast. I said yes because I thought he was asking if I was okay. Nobody asked me if I wanted Spanish.
Other accounts:
Recorded statement transcript extract (Record or log):
Adjuster: "So you didn't stop at the sign?" Insured: "Yes." Adjuster: "Okay, and the other car had the right of way?" Insured: "Yes, yes, okay." No interpreter offered. Duration 6 minutes.

Doorbell camera summary (Record or log):
Her car slows to a near stop at the line, then pulls forward. The other car enters the frame at speed from the right, without slowing, about 1.5 seconds before impact.
Damage: Her Altima: front-right corner, $3,600. Other car: driver's side.
Third parties: The other driver and their insurer
Evidence:
Recorded statement transcript
Doorbell camera footage
Photos of both cars
What happened (answer): She did essentially stop. Her "yes" answers came from a language misunderstanding, and the fault decision rested on them.
Missing information (answer):
The other driver's speed
A statement from her taken with a qualified interpreter
Inconsistencies (answer): The transcript records her agreeing she did not stop; the camera shows she slowed to a near stop
Innocent explanations (answer): People answering in a second language often say yes to show they are listening
Questions to ask (answer):
Retake her statement in Spanish with a qualified interpreter
Ask the other driver about his speed
Next steps (answer):
Do not rely on the English statement: it was taken without checking her language needs
Retake the statement with a qualified interpreter, and record her language preference on the file
Re-decide fault on the camera footage and the new statement; the other driver’s speed may make fault shared or his
Apologize, explain the review, and correct any fault record or premium effect
Assessment (answer): Disputed, but the fault decision is unsafe: it rests on a statement she did not understand, and the independent camera contradicts it.
Recommended action (answer): Retake the statement with an interpreter, reopen the fault decision on the camera evidence, and correct the record.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Fault changed to 50/50 after review; record corrected
Other driver found mainly at fault for speeding; recovery made
Tags: Texas, interpreter, recorded statement, language access, fault decision, doorbell camera

Title: Told the agent on WhatsApp the same day, registered 38 days later
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder's car was scraped along its side by a private bus at a junction in Visakhapatnam. When nobody came I phoned the company myself. The car is standing in my parking exactly as it was, nothing has been touched.
Other accounts:
WhatsApp messages with the agent (Message or email):
Accident day, 19:42: four photos of the damage and "Sir bus scraped my car at Siripuram junction, please register claim". 19:58, agent: "noted sir, will register". No further messages for five weeks.

Insurer claim record (Record or log):
Claim registered 38 days after the accident date via the call centre. Remark: late intimation, refer to claims manager. Agent code linked to the policy.
Damage: Hyundai i20: left doors, rear quarter panel and mirror scraped and dented; estimate ₹46,000. Unrepaired.
Third parties: The private bus operator
Evidence:
WhatsApp messages with time stamps and photos
Insurer claim record
Unrepaired car available for survey

Ask the agent why the claim was not registered
Ask whether he noted the bus number

Treat the date of the WhatsApp message to the agent as the date of intimation: the agent acts for the insurer and the delay is not the policyholder’s
Arrange a survey now; the car is unrepaired, so nothing has been lost by the delay
Settle on merit within the regulator’s timelines once the survey report is in
Take up the agent’s failure with the agency team
Assessment (answer): Genuine claim, intimated in time to the insurer's agent. The delay causes no prejudice and should not be held against him.
Recommended action (answer): Condone the delay, survey and settle, and address the agent's lapse.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Survey done next day; claim settled
Agent counselled and the WhatsApp channel added to the claims intake process

Title: A road test by the service centre, and a motorcyclist in hospital
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder left her car at an authorised service centre in Chennai for a noise in the suspension. During the afternoon the car hit a motorcyclist on Anna Salai, who suffered a fractured leg. The service centre says the policyholder's son was driving with a technician beside him.
