Job card: "Customer complaint: noise from front suspension. Road test by technician before and after work." Gate register: out 14:10, driver name of a service centre technician, purpose "road test"; in 15:35.

Service centre manager (Statement):
The customer's son came to check the car and asked to drive it on the road test. Our technician was in the passenger seat. The customer's policy should cover it, it is her car.
Damage: Motorcyclist: fractured tibia, surgery. Policyholder's car: front bumper and bonnet, ₹38,000. Motorcycle: front fork and wheel.
Third parties:
Injured motorcyclist and his family
The authorised service centre and its motor trade insurer
Evidence:
Job card
Gate register
Service centre manager's statement
Tribunal claim petition
What happened (answer): The car was being driven on a road test by the service centre in connection with its trade. Who was at the wheel is disputed, but the use was the service centre's.
Missing information (answer):
The son's college attendance record for that afternoon
CCTV from the service centre gate
The service centre’s motor trade policy
Inconsistencies (answer):
The manager says the son drove; the gate register names the technician as driver
The policyholder says her son was in college all day
Innocent explanations (answer): A manager may genuinely believe a family member was present if someone came to collect paperwork
Questions to ask (answer):
Ask the college for the son’s attendance that afternoon
Ask the service centre for its gate CCTV and its motor trade policy
Next steps (answer):
Establish who drove from the gate register, CCTV and the son’s attendance record
Note that the standard private car policy excludes use for any purpose in connection with the motor trade; a road test during servicing is such a use, so the service centre’s motor trade policy should respond
Defend the tribunal claim on that basis, but if the tribunal makes the owner’s insurer satisfy the award, seek recovery from the service centre and its insurer
Settle the owner’s own damage through the service centre, which had custody of the car
Assessment (answer): Disputed on who drove, but the documents point to the technician. The use was the service centre's, so primary responsibility lies with its motor trade cover.
Recommended action (answer): Gather the gate CCTV and attendance record, put the service centre's insurer on notice, and protect the injured rider's claim while liability is sorted out.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Tribunal holds the service centre’s insurer liable; owner’s insurer released
Award paid by the owner’s insurer and recovered from the service centre
Tags: motor trade, service centre, road test, limitation as to use, job card, MACT

Title: He opted out of the ₹15 lakh cover because he had another one
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder, aged 52, died when a lorry ran into the back of his scooter on the outer ring road in Mysuru. His widow has claimed the ₹15 lakh owner-driver personal accident cover under the scooter's policy. The policy shows he opted out of that cover at purchase, declaring that he held a separate personal accident policy of ₹15 lakh. That separate policy lapsed two months before the accident and was not renewed.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): My husband always took insurance seriously. He said he had a bigger accident policy from his office so he didn't need it twice. I didn't know the other one had stopped. Now I have two children in college. The lorry driver ran away but the police found the lorry.
Other accounts:
Motor policy schedule (Document):
Two-wheeler package policy. Compulsory personal accident cover for owner-driver: not opted. Declaration signed by the insured: "I hold a general personal accident policy with a sum insured of ₹15 lakh or more."

Police report extract (Report):
Lorry hit the scooter from behind at about 22:00. Driver fled; lorry traced the next day and seized. Case registered against the lorry driver for rash and negligent driving causing death.
Damage: Death of the owner-driver. Scooter damaged beyond repair.
Third parties:
The lorry driver and owner
The lorry's insurer
Evidence:
Policy schedule with the opt-out declaration
Police report
Death certificate
Lapse notice of the separate PA policy
What happened (answer): He opted out of the owner-driver personal accident cover in good faith, relying on a policy that later lapsed. The motor policy has no personal accident cover to pay.
Missing information (answer):
Whether the employer’s group personal accident cover still applied
The lorry’s insurance details
Innocent explanations (answer): Many owners opt out because they believe an employer cover protects them
Questions to ask (answer):
Ask the family whether his employer had any group accident cover in force
Get the lorry’s insurance details from the police
Next steps (answer):
Explain kindly that the scooter’s policy does not include the owner-driver personal accident cover because he opted out
Pay the own-damage claim for the scooter under the package policy
Help the family check any employer group cover, and explain their right to claim compensation from the lorry’s insurer before the motor accident claims tribunal
Check that the opt-out declaration was properly taken at sale
Assessment (answer): Genuine and tragic, but the personal accident benefit was not bought. The family's main remedy is the claim against the lorry's insurer.
Recommended action (answer): Decline the personal accident benefit with care, pay the scooter, and guide the family to the tribunal claim and any employer cover.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Family receives compensation through the tribunal claim against the lorry’s insurer
Employer group cover found and paid
Tags: compulsory personal accident, owner-driver, opt-out declaration, standalone PA policy, nominee, MACT

Title: Wedding guests in the back of a Tata Ace
Accident type: Single vehicle or loss of control
Claim notification (exhibit A): A Tata Ace mini truck insured as a goods carriage was carrying nine wedding guests in its cargo area when it overturned on a bend near Bhilwara, Rajasthan. Two passengers died and six were injured. The families have filed claims before the motor accident claims tribunal against the owner and the insurer. The policy covers liability to third parties and to the owner of the goods travelling with them, not to passengers carried free of charge.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): It was my cousin's wedding and the jeep we booked didn't come. Everyone asked me to take them to the village in my Ace. I said it isn't for people but they insisted. The road bent suddenly and the back swung out. I will never forgive myself.
Other accounts:
Police report extract (Report):
Goods vehicle carrying 9 persons in the cargo body and 2 in the cabin overturned on a curve. Two deaths at the spot, six injured. Driver-owner holds a valid licence for the vehicle class. No goods on board.

Policy schedule (Document):
Goods carrying commercial vehicle, liability only plus own damage. Limitations as to use: carriage of goods. Persons covered beyond third parties: owner of goods or their representative travelling in the vehicle. No cover for other passengers.
Damage: Two deaths and six injured passengers. Tata Ace overturned, cabin and body damaged.
Third parties:
Families of the two deceased passengers
Six injured passengers
Evidence:
Police report
Policy schedule and limitations as to use
Tribunal claim petitions
What happened (answer): The owner-driver used a goods vehicle to carry passengers free of charge, in breach of the policy, and lost control on a bend.
Missing information (answer):
Post-mortem reports and medical records for the injured
Whether any passenger paid a fare
Innocent explanations (answer): In rural areas goods vehicles are often pressed into service when booked transport fails
Questions to ask (answer): Confirm whether anyone paid to travel, which would change the analysis to hire or reward
Next steps (answer):
Defend the claims on the policy breach: the policy does not cover gratuitous passengers in a goods vehicle
Expect the tribunal may still direct the insurer to satisfy the awards first and recover the amount from the owner; plan for that recovery
Decline the own-damage claim for use outside the permitted purpose
Treat the families with care in all communication; they are victims, not the policyholder
Assessment (answer): Genuine tragedy caused by an unlawful use of a goods vehicle. The insurer has a strong policy defence against the passenger claims, but may have to pay first and recover from the owner.
Recommended action (answer): Contest liability on the breach, prepare for any order to pay first, and pursue recovery from the owner.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Tribunal orders the insurer to pay the awards and recover from the owner
Insurer exonerated; awards fall on the owner
Tags: goods carriage, gratuitous passengers, policy breach, MACT, recovery from owner, overloading

Title: A driving licence that Sarathi has never heard of
Claim notification (exhibit A): A truck belonging to a transport company in Nagpur ran into the back of a car in fog on the Nagpur–Amravati highway, injuring two occupants. The truck's driver had worked for the company for 14 months. After the accident the licence he had produced turned out not to exist on the Sarathi licence database. The company says it inspected his licence card, made him take a driving test and checked his previous employer before hiring him.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): We have thirty trucks and we check every driver. He showed us his card, he drove for an hour with our senior driver, and his old employer said he was good. He had no accidents in fourteen months. How are we supposed to know a card is fake when it looks real?
Other accounts:
Sarathi database check (Record or log):
Licence number produced by the driver: no record found. No licence of any class issued in the driver's name in the state shown on the card.

Company hiring file (Document):
Copy of the licence card. Driving test report signed by the senior driver, rated good. Reference call note from the previous employer. Appointment letter 14 months before the accident.
Damage: Car occupants: one fracture, one soft-tissue injury. Car: rear end, ₹2,10,000. Truck: front bumper and grille.
Third parties:
Two injured car occupants
The driver
Evidence:
Sarathi check
Company hiring file
Police report
Tribunal claim petitions
What happened (answer): The driver deceived his employer with a fake licence. The company took reasonable care in hiring him but did not verify the licence online.
Missing information (answer): Whether the company could have verified the licence online at the time of hiring
Fraud indicators (answer): Licence with no record on the national database
Innocent explanations (answer): A good-quality fake card can deceive an employer who checks the card and tests the driver
Questions to ask (answer): Ask the company whether it had any process to verify licences online
Next steps (answer):
Satisfy the third-party claims: the insurer can only avoid liability against the owner if it proves the owner failed to take reasonable care over the licence, which the hiring file makes hard
Decide the truck’s own damage with legal advice: the driver clause is breached on its face, but the owner’s due diligence weighs against repudiation
Report the fake licence to the police
Advise the company to verify all licences on the national database
Assessment (answer): Genuine accident; the owner is a victim of the driver's deception and took reasonable care. Third-party liability stands; avoiding cover against the owner would be hard to justify.
Recommended action (answer): Pay the third parties, take a reasoned decision on own damage, and report the fake licence.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Third parties paid; own damage paid after legal review
Tribunal refuses the insurer’s plea to be exonerated
Tags: fake driving licence, due diligence, driver clause, Sarathi, transport company, MACT

Title: The surveyor recommends repudiation because the PUC had expired
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder's car was rear-ended by a tempo at a signal in Pune in the rain. She has claimed for the repairs under her own policy. The surveyor's report confirms the damage is consistent with the accident and assesses it at ₹54,000, but adds: "PUC certificate expired three months before the accident. Recommend repudiation." She renewed the PUC the day after the accident.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): The PUC slipped my mind, I'm usually careful. I got it done the next day and the car passed easily. I don't see what pollution has to do with a tempo hitting me from behind. The tempo driver admitted it.
Other accounts:
Surveyor’s report extract (Report):
Damage to rear bumper, boot lid and tail lamps consistent with a rear impact. Assessed loss ₹54,000. Driving licence and registration valid. PUC certificate expired three months before the accident. Recommend repudiation.

Tempo driver (Witness account):
The road was wet and my brakes didn't hold. I hit her car from behind. I gave her my owner's number.
Damage: Honda City: rear bumper, boot lid and tail lamps, assessed ₹54,000.
Third parties: Tempo driver and its owner
Evidence:
Surveyor's report
Tempo driver's statement
New PUC certificate issued the next day
What happened (answer): A genuine rear-end collision. The lapsed pollution certificate has nothing to do with the loss and is not a ground to deny the claim.
Missing information (answer): The tempo's insurance details
Innocent explanations (answer): Pollution certificates are easy to let lapse
Questions to ask (answer): Ask for the tempo owner's details for recovery
Next steps (answer):
Do not repudiate: IRDAI clarified in August 2020 that not holding a valid PUC certificate is not a valid reason to deny a motor claim
Settle the assessed loss within seven days of the survey report
Remind her that a valid PUC is needed at renewal and is a legal requirement for driving
Correct the surveyor’s recommendation in the file
Assessment (answer): Genuine and payable. The PUC lapse is a traffic offence, not a policy ground for refusal.
Recommended action (answer): Settle ₹54,000 less any excess, and correct the repudiation recommendation.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Claim settled within a week
Surveyor’s report template updated
Tags: PUC certificate, pollution under control, IRDAI clarification, surveyor report, repudiation, own damage

Title: Depreciation at 40% on a car that was four and a half years old
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder's SUV hit a road divider in Lucknow after swerving for a stray dog. It was first registered on 11 March 2021 and the accident happened on 2 October 2025. His policy has no zero-depreciation add-on. The settlement letter deducts depreciation of 40% on metal parts, 50% on plastic parts, 50% on the windscreen and 50% on paint materials. He says the deductions are too high.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): I know I don't have zero dep, the agent explained that. But 40% on the bonnet and 50% on the windscreen? My car isn't even five years old. A friend at another company says glass has no depreciation at all.
Other accounts:
Assessment sheet extract (Document):
Bonnet, front fender (metal): depreciation 40%. Front bumper (plastic): 50%. Windscreen (glass): 50%. Paint materials: 50%. Labour: nil. Vehicle age taken as "5 years".

Registration certificate (Record or log):
Date of first registration: 11 March 2021.
Damage: Creta: bonnet, front fender, front bumper and windscreen. Metal parts ₹64,000, plastic ₹18,000, windscreen ₹14,000, paint materials ₹9,000, labour ₹16,000.
Third parties: None
Evidence:
Assessment sheet
Registration certificate
Repair invoice
What happened (answer): A genuine accident. The assessment used the wrong vehicle age for metal parts and wrongly depreciated the glass.
Missing information (answer): The surveyor’s working for the vehicle age
Inconsistencies (answer): The sheet takes the age as 5 years; the car was 4 years and about 7 months old
Innocent explanations (answer): Rounding the age up is a common error in assessment sheets
Questions to ask (answer): Ask the surveyor to recompute the age from the date of first registration
Next steps (answer):
Recompute the age: 4 years and about 7 months, so metal parts take 35% depreciation, not 40%
Apply nil depreciation to glass parts, 50% to plastic and rubber parts, and 50% to paint materials only
Pay the difference with a revised assessment sheet that shows each rate
Check for the same error in the surveyor’s other assessments
Assessment (answer): Genuine claim, wrongly assessed. Under the standard depreciation schedule metal parts at this age take 35% and glass takes none.
Recommended action (answer): Revise the assessment at the correct rates and pay the difference.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Revised settlement adds about ₹10,200
Complaint closed after the revised sheet is sent
Tags: depreciation, metal parts, glass, vehicle age, surveyor assessment, no zero depreciation

Title: An auto worth ₹1.2 lakh, a repair bill of ₹96,000, and a family that needs it back
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder's CNG auto-rickshaw was hit on its side by a private bus in heavy rain in Chennai. Its insured declared value is ₹1,20,000. The surveyor assessed repairs at ₹96,000, which is 80% of the insured value, and proposed treating it as a constructive total loss. The owner wants it repaired. A week later his garage sent a revised estimate of ₹88,000, replacing new parts with refurbished ones.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): This auto feeds my family. If you take it away, getting a new one and the permit sorted will take months. My garage can fix it. I asked them to bring the estimate down so you would allow the repair. I just want to get back on the road.
Other accounts:
Surveyor’s report extract (Report):
Chassis bent on the left side, body shell and roof frame damaged, CNG cylinder mounting distorted. Repair cost ₹96,000 against IDV ₹1,20,000: exceeds 75%. Recommend constructive total loss.

Revised garage estimate (Document):
Chassis straightening instead of replacement. Refurbished roof frame and refurbished CNG cylinder bracket. Total ₹88,000.
Damage: Auto-rickshaw: chassis, body shell, roof frame and CNG cylinder mounting damaged.
Third parties: The private bus operator and its insurer
Evidence:
Surveyor's report
Revised garage estimate
Photos
What happened (answer): A genuine accident that pushes the repair cost past 75% of the insured value. The lower estimate was produced to avoid a total loss, partly with refurbished safety-related parts.
Missing information (answer): The bus operator's insurance details for recovery
Inconsistencies (answer): The revised estimate cuts the cost by using refurbished parts, including a CNG cylinder bracket
Innocent explanations (answer): An owner desperate to keep his livelihood will naturally push for a cheaper repair
Questions to ask (answer): Ask the owner whether he would accept a settlement that lets him keep the vehicle and repair it himself
Next steps (answer):
Do not accept the refurbished CNG cylinder bracket or a straightened chassis without an engineer’s approval: they are safety-critical on a CNG vehicle
Treat it as a constructive total loss on the surveyor’s figures, since repair exceeds 75% of the insured value
Offer a settlement on a net-of-salvage basis so he keeps the vehicle and can repair it at his own garage
Explain the options plainly and settle quickly; pursue the bus operator’s insurer
Assessment (answer): Genuine claim; a constructive total loss. A net-of-salvage settlement meets his need to keep the auto without accepting an unsafe estimate.
Recommended action (answer): Settle as a total loss net of salvage, let him keep and repair the vehicle, and recover from the bus operator.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Settled net of salvage; auto repaired and back on the road in three weeks
Owner chooses the full IDV and buys a new auto
Tags: auto-rickshaw, constructive total loss, IDV, 75% rule, net of salvage, livelihood

Title: Halfway through a cashless repair, the garage was delisted
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder's car was taken to a network garage in Bengaluru after a collision at a junction. The insurer approved a cashless repair of ₹1,42,000 after the survey. Midway through the repair the insurer delisted the garage over billing disputes on other claims. The garage now says it will not release the car unless she pays the full ₹1,42,000 herself and claims it back.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): Your company sent me to that garage and approved the repair. Now I'm told it's not your garage any more and I have to pay one lakh forty-two thousand to get my own car back. I don't have that kind of money lying around. I've been taking autos to work for three weeks.
Other accounts:
Cashless approval (Document):
Cashless approval for ₹1,42,000 issued 9 days after the accident, subject to final bill and re-inspection. Garage status at approval: network.

Network team notice (Record or log):
Garage delisted with immediate effect from 16 days after the accident. Instruction: no new cashless claims. No instruction on claims already approved.
Damage: Baleno: front end, radiator and airbag module. Approved repair ₹1,42,000.
Third parties: The delisted garage
Evidence:
Cashless approval
Network team notice
Garage’s demand for payment
What happened (answer): A genuine claim caught by the insurer's own delisting decision. The repair was approved while the garage was in the network.
Missing information (answer): Re-inspection of the completed repair
Innocent explanations (answer): The garage is protecting itself after losing its network status; holding the car is leverage, not evidence of wrongdoing on this claim
Questions to ask (answer): Ask the garage how much of the approved work is complete
Next steps (answer):
Honour the cashless approval for the work already authorised: it was given while the garage was in the network, and the delisting was the insurer’s decision
Re-inspect, then pay the garage directly against the final bill so the car is released without her paying
If the garage refuses, settle her reimbursement within seven days of receiving the documents
Fix the delisting process so approved claims are handled before a garage is removed
Assessment (answer): Genuine claim; the problem was created by the insurer. The customer should not have to fund the repair.
Recommended action (answer): Pay the garage directly under the existing approval and get the car released.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Car released within two days after direct payment
Process changed so approved claims are completed before delisting
Tags: cashless, network garage, delisting, reimbursement, vehicle release, customer impact

Title: One key for the stolen Scorpio, and a duplicate cut three weeks earlier
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder reported his Mahindra Scorpio stolen from outside his house in Rohini, Delhi, overnight. An FIR was registered the next morning and the insurer was informed the same day. For settlement he has produced one key and says the second was lost two years ago on a trek in Himachal. The authorised dealer's records show a duplicate key was cut at his request three weeks before the theft.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): The second key fell in a river near Kasol two years ago, my friends were there. I don't remember any duplicate key. Maybe the dealer has the wrong car. The police say these Scorpios are stolen to order.
Other accounts:
Dealer service record (Record or log):
Duplicate key programmed 23 days before the theft. Request in the customer's name, paid in cash. Vehicle brought in by a person signing as "driver".

Police status (Report):
FIR registered for theft of the vehicle. Investigation ongoing; vehicle not traced. Final report not yet filed.
Damage: Scorpio stolen; IDV ₹11,80,000.
Third parties:
Authorised dealer
The person who brought the car in for the duplicate key
Evidence:
FIR
Dealer service record
One key
Police status
What happened (answer): The theft may be genuine, but a duplicate key cut three weeks before, which he does not mention, needs explaining before settlement.
Missing information (answer):
The duplicate key
Who the "driver" was
Dealer CCTV of the day the key was cut
The non-traceable report from the police and court
Inconsistencies (answer): He says he knows nothing of a duplicate key; the dealer cut one at his request three weeks before
Fraud indicators (answer):
Duplicate key made shortly before the theft
Only one key produced
Cash payment by an unnamed driver
Innocent explanations (answer):
A driver or family member may have ordered the key without telling him
Thieves sometimes obtain keys by deception at dealers
Questions to ask (answer):
Ask whether he employs a driver and who took the car to the dealer
Ask the dealer for CCTV and the signature on the request
Next steps (answer):
Put the dealer record to him and take a written explanation
Investigate the duplicate key with the dealer’s CCTV and the signature
Do not settle until the explanation is checked and the non-traceable report is received; then decide on merit
Collect the remaining settlement documents in parallel: the RC, the remaining key, transfer forms and subrogation letter
Assessment (answer): Suspicious, not proven. The undisclosed duplicate key is the central question; it may have an innocent answer through a driver.
Recommended action (answer): Investigate the duplicate key before settlement and keep the theft paperwork moving.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Driver admits ordering the key and is arrested with a gang; claim paid
Claim repudiated after CCTV shows the policyholder at the dealer
Tags: theft, missing key, duplicate key, non-traceable report, settlement documents, dealer records

Title: Loan closed in March, bank still on the RC in October
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder's car was declared a total loss after a head-on collision on a highway near Jaipur. The registration certificate still shows hypothecation to a co-operative bank. She repaid the loan in March and has the bank's no-objection certificate and a zero-dues letter, but never had the hypothecation removed at the RTO. The settlement team says it can only pay the bank.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): I finished paying in March, I have the letters. The bank says it has no claim on my car. Why should the money go to them and come back to me in a few weeks? I need it to put down on another car.
Other accounts:
Bank letters (Document):
No-objection certificate for termination of hypothecation, dated in March, with Form 35 signed by the bank. Separate letter confirming the loan account is closed with no dues.

Registration certificate (Record or log):
Hypothecated to the co-operative bank. No termination endorsed.
Damage: Car total loss; IDV ₹6,40,000.
Third parties:
The co-operative bank
The other driver
Evidence:
Bank NOC and Form 35
Zero-dues letter
Registration certificate
What happened (answer): A genuine total loss where the loan is paid off but the hypothecation entry was never removed.
Missing information (answer): Confirmation from the bank direct, not only through the customer
Innocent explanations (answer): Many owners never get round to removing hypothecation after closing a loan
Questions to ask (answer): Confirm with the bank directly that the loan is closed
Next steps (answer):
Verify the NOC and zero-dues letter with the bank directly
Once verified, pay the settlement to her, with the bank’s written consent on file
Collect the transfer documents for the salvage, including the bank’s Form 35
Explain the timeline to her so she can plan the new purchase
Assessment (answer): Genuine and straightforward once the bank confirms. Paying the bank would add delay for no purpose.
Recommended action (answer): Verify with the bank and pay her directly.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Bank confirms; settlement paid to her within a week
Bank insists on joint cheque; paid jointly and released the same day
Tags: hypothecation, financier, NOC, Form 35, total loss, payee

Title: Treated free under the scheme, then billed to us as well
Claim notification (exhibit A): Our policyholder's car hit a pedestrian, Mr Patil, on a road in Nashik. He was taken to a designated hospital and treated for six days under the government's cashless treatment scheme for road accident victims. The hospital has now sent our claims team a bill of ₹1,52,000 for "direct settlement" of the same admission. Mr Patil's lawyer has also included the same hospital bills in his claim before the motor accident claims tribunal.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): (Lawyer for Mr Patil) My client suffered a fractured femur and was in hospital for six days. The hospital bills are part of his medical expenses and are claimed in full from the insurer of the vehicle, along with his loss of earnings and pain and suffering.
Other accounts:
Cashless scheme portal record (Record or log):
Victim admitted under the Cashless Treatment of Road Accident Victims Scheme, 2025. Treatment package approved and paid to the hospital: ₹1,38,000 for six days from the date of the accident. Status: settled by the State Health Agency.

Hospital bill sent to the insurer (Document):
Inpatient bill for the same admission dates: ₹1,52,000. Request: direct settlement by the insurer of the offending vehicle. No mention of the scheme payment.
Damage: Pedestrian: fractured femur, six days in hospital, about three months off work.
Third parties:
Sunil Patil
His lawyer
The designated hospital
Evidence:
Cashless scheme portal record
Hospital bill sent to the insurer
Tribunal claim petition
What happened (answer): The hospital was paid for this treatment under the scheme and has billed the insurer again for the same admission. The lawyer has probably included the bills without knowing the scheme paid them.
Missing information (answer):
Any treatment after the seven days the scheme covers
Proof of his earnings
Inconsistencies (answer): The hospital was paid ₹1,38,000 by the scheme for the same admission it now bills at ₹1,52,000
Fraud indicators (answer):
Same admission billed twice
No mention of the scheme payment in the bill
Innocent explanations (answer):
Hospital billing teams may not link scheme payments to later insurer requests
Lawyers often claim all bills given to them by the family
Questions to ask (answer):
Ask the hospital to explain the bill against the scheme payment
Ask the lawyer for any treatment costs after the scheme period
Next steps (answer):
Do not pay the hospital’s bill: the admission was already paid under the scheme
In the tribunal claim, ask that medical expenses met by the scheme be excluded, so compensation is not paid twice
Report the duplicate bill to the State Health Agency
Handle the rest of the claim on merit: loss of earnings, pain and suffering and any later treatment
Assessment (answer): The injury claim is genuine; the medical bill is a duplicate. The hospital's request is suspicious, not proven fraud, and the lawyer's inclusion is probably an error.
Recommended action (answer): Refuse the duplicate bill, exclude scheme-paid expenses in the tribunal claim, and settle the remaining heads on evidence.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Hospital withdraws its bill; claim settled without the duplicate expenses
State Health Agency investigates the hospital’s billing
Tags: cashless treatment scheme 2025, golden hour, designated hospital, double billing, MACT, medical expenses

Title: Five lakh without proving fault, or more if they can
Claim notification (exhibit A): Our policyholder's truck hit and killed Raju Yadav, aged 32, a construction worker, as he crossed a road on the outskirts of Patna in fog at dawn. His widow filed a claim for the fixed no-fault compensation of ₹5 lakh under section 164 of the Motor Vehicles Act. Her lawyer now says she will also file a fault-based claim under section 166 for loss of dependency, which could be several times larger.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): He earned about fifteen thousand a month on the sites and sent everything home. We have two small children and his mother. People told me to file the five lakh first because it is quick. Now the lawyer says we can get more. I don't understand which one we should do.
Other accounts:
Police report extract (Report):
Pedestrian struck by a truck in dense fog at about 05:40 while crossing the road. Driver states he could not see. Truck speed not established. No pedestrian crossing nearby. Case registered for causing death by negligence.

Claim petition under section 164 (Document):
Claim for fixed compensation of ₹5,00,000 for death, without pleading fault. Filed by the widow on behalf of the dependants.
Damage: Death of a 32-year-old earner with four dependants.
Third parties:
Sunita Yadav and the dependants
Their lawyer
Evidence:
Police report
Section 164 claim petition
Death certificate
Proof of dependants
What happened (answer): A genuine fatal accident. The family has started a no-fault claim and is weighing a larger fault-based claim; the law does not allow full compensation under both for the same death.
Missing information (answer):
Proof of his earnings
Evidence of the truck’s speed and lights in the fog
Innocent explanations (answer): Families often file the quick no-fault claim first on advice from others, before understanding the alternative
Questions to ask (answer): Ask the lawyer which remedy the family will pursue
Next steps (answer):
Explain, through the designated officer, that section 164 gives fixed compensation without proving fault, and that the family cannot also receive full fault-based compensation under section 166 for the same death
If they pursue section 166, assess fault realistically: dense fog and a truck driver who could not see do not clear the driver
Make a fair settlement offer on the basis the family chooses, with earnings and dependency properly assessed
Do not exploit their uncertainty; record the advice given
Assessment (answer): Genuine fatal claim. The task is to handle the choice of remedy fairly and avoid double compensation, while recognising the driver probably bears fault.
Recommended action (answer): Clarify the election of remedy and make a fair offer on the chosen route.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Family withdraws the section 164 claim and settles under section 166 for ₹26 lakh
Family takes the ₹5 lakh quickly and closes the matter
Tags: section 164, no-fault compensation, section 166, fault-based claim, designated officer, election of remedy

Title: The detailed accident report arrived on day 88, and the offer is due
Claim notification (exhibit A): Our policyholder's car hit a motorcyclist, Imran Sheikh, aged 38, at a junction in Indore; he died in hospital. The police filed the Detailed Accident Report with the claims tribunal 88 days after the accident and served a copy on the insurer. The report records his income as ₹45,000 a month from a mobile repair shop. No income tax returns are on file; his bank statements show average deposits of about ₹18,000 a month. The insurer's designated officer has not yet acted, and 24 of the 30 days for an offer have passed.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): (Widow) His shop was always full, he repaired phones for the whole market. He kept most of the money in cash, he didn't trust banks. We have three children. My husband was everything to us.
Other accounts:
Detailed Accident Report extract (Report):
Accident at a junction; car driver failed to yield. Deceased aged 38, self-employed, monthly income stated by the family as ₹45,000. Dependants: widow, three minor children. Documents: bank statements; no income tax returns.

Bank statement summary (Record or log):
Savings account in the deceased's name, 24 months: average monthly credits ₹18,200, mostly cash deposits.
Damage: Death of a 38-year-old self-employed earner with four dependants.
Third parties:
The widow and three children
Their lawyer
Evidence:
Detailed Accident Report
Bank statements
Post-mortem report
What happened (answer): A genuine fatal accident caused by our policyholder. The stated income is higher than the evidence supports, and the insurer is close to missing its time limit for an offer.
Missing information (answer):
Shop rent agreement or trade licence
GST or other business records
Inconsistencies (answer): Income stated at ₹45,000 a month; bank credits average ₹18,200
Fraud indicators (answer): Income stated without documentary support
Innocent explanations (answer): Small traders often keep income in cash and do not file returns
Questions to ask (answer): Ask for the shop’s rent agreement, trade licence and any supplier invoices
Next steps (answer):
Make the designated officer’s offer before the 30 days from receipt of the report run out
Base income on the evidence, with a reasoned view of cash income, rather than the stated ₹45,000
Calculate dependency in the standard way: income plus future prospects for a self-employed person under 40, a deduction for personal expenses for four dependants, the multiplier for age 38, and the conventional heads
Present the offer to the tribunal with the reasoning, so it can be accepted or adjudicated quickly
Assessment (answer): Genuine fatal claim with an overstated income. The urgent risk is procedural: missing the 30-day offer window.
Recommended action (answer): Make a reasoned offer within the deadline on evidence-based income.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Offer on ₹24,000 a month accepted before the tribunal
Tribunal fixes income at ₹27,000 and awards accordingly

Offending car identified through CCTV seven months after the accident. Owner and driver traced; driver arrested. Vehicle insured on the date of the accident.

Family of Gopal Das

Claims Settlement Commissioner

Tribunal claim petition

Title: A dented roof on a brand-new Seltos, and two companies blaming each other
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder bought a new Kia Seltos from a dealer in Kochi with home delivery. His policy started on the invoice date. A transport company delivered the car on a car carrier. At delivery he noticed a dented roof and a scratched door. The transporter says the damage happened in the dealer's yard; the dealer says the car left the yard perfect. He has claimed under his policy and the insurer wants to recover the cost from whoever is responsible.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): The roof was dented right above the driver's door, like something hit it from above. I wrote "damaged, subject to inspection" on the delivery note before I signed. I don't care who pays as long as my new car is fixed properly.
Other accounts:
Dealer’s yard dispatch photos (Record or log):
Four photos time-stamped at dispatch, showing the car from both sides. Roof not visible in any photo. Doors on the visible side unmarked.

Transport company’s delivery note (Document):
Loaded at dealer's yard at 10:15. Delivered at 15:40. Customer remark: "Roof dented, door scratched, subject to inspection." Driver remark: "Damage present at loading."
Damage: Seltos: roof dent above the driver's door and a scratched rear door; estimate ₹68,000 including roof repaint.
Third parties:
The dealer
The transport company
Evidence:
Dealer dispatch photos
Delivery note with both remarks
Policyholder's photos at delivery
What happened (answer): The damage happened before or during delivery. Whether it was at the yard or on the carrier is genuinely unclear, but either way the policyholder did not cause it.
Missing information (answer):
The car carrier’s upper deck layout and loading photos
Yard CCTV
Inconsistencies (answer): The driver says the damage was present at loading; the dealer says the car left perfect, but its photos do not show the roof
Innocent explanations (answer): Roof damage from an upper-deck car carrier and yard knocks both happen
Questions to ask (answer):
Ask the transporter which deck the car travelled on and for loading photos
Ask the dealer for yard CCTV
Next steps (answer):
Pay the policyholder’s repair: the loss happened after the policy started and he did not cause it
Serve a written notice of claim on both the transporter and the dealer promptly, preserving recovery rights, including under carriage law against the transporter
Use the roof-shaped dent, deck position and CCTV to decide where the damage occurred
Pursue recovery against the party the evidence points to, or settle a split if it remains unclear
Assessment (answer): Disputed between two businesses, not with the customer. Pay him promptly and pursue recovery on the evidence.
Recommended action (answer): Settle the claim and serve notice on both the transporter and the dealer.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Transporter’s loading photos show an upper-deck strike; full recovery
Recovery shared 50/50 after neither side’s evidence settles it
Tags: new car delivery, car carrier, transit damage, recovery, delivery note, common carrier

Title: Five accidents, five cars that were scrapped last year
Accident type: Single vehicle or loss of control
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder claims ₹3.8 lakh for a 2017 Honda City damaged in a crash into a divider near Ghaziabad. The policy was bought online with an uploaded RC copy. A Vahan check shows the chassis number belongs to a car deregistered at a registered vehicle scrapping facility last year, with a certificate of deposit issued. The claims team has found four other claims in six months with the same pattern, all repaired at the same garage and all linked to the same mobile number.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): I bought this car second-hand from a man in Meerut, I have the papers. I don't know anything about any scrapping. The garage is near my house, everybody uses it. Please send the surveyor again if you don't believe me.
Other accounts:
Vahan record (Record or log):
Chassis number status: scrapped. Certificate of deposit issued by a registered vehicle scrapping facility 11 months before the policy. Registration cancelled.

Claims analytics note (Report):
Five own-damage claims in six months: all policies bought online with uploaded RC copies; all chassis numbers match scrapped vehicles; all repaired at the same garage in Ghaziabad; the same mobile number appears as alternate contact on four policies. Surveyor photos show chassis number plates with fresh rivets.
Damage: Claimed ₹3.8 lakh for front end damage. Four related claims total about ₹14 lakh.
Third parties:
The garage
The person behind the shared mobile number
The registered vehicle scrapping facility
Evidence:
Vahan records for all five vehicles
Claims analytics note
Surveyor's photos of the chassis plates
Uploaded RC copies
What happened (answer): An organised group is insuring cars carrying the identities of scrapped vehicles, using forged RCs, and claiming for staged damage through one garage.
Missing information (answer):
The scrapping facility’s records of what happened to the scrapped bodies and plates
The real engine and chassis numbers stamped on the car
Inconsistencies (answer): The uploaded RC shows an active registration; Vahan shows the vehicle scrapped and the registration cancelled
Fraud indicators (answer):
Identity of a scrapped vehicle
Fresh rivets on the chassis number plate
Linked claims through one garage and one mobile number
Innocent explanations (answer): A buyer could unknowingly purchase a re-plated car, but not five times through the same garage
Questions to ask (answer):
Have the actual chassis and engine numbers stamped on the car read by an expert
Ask the policyholder for the seller’s details and the payment record
Next steps (answer):
Hold all five claims and refer them together to the fraud investigation unit
Inspect the vehicles for the stamped numbers and compare them with Vahan
Report to the police and the transport authority, and alert the scrapping facility
Cancel the policies obtained on forged documents and share the pattern through industry fraud channels
Assessment (answer): Organised fraud: scrapped identities, forged registration documents and a common garage across five claims.
Recommended action (answer): Hold and investigate all five claims together, report to the police, and void the policies.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Police find a workshop re-plating salvage cars; claims repudiated
Garage owner and two agents arrested
Tags: scrapped vehicle, certificate of deposit, Vahan, forged RC, same garage, organised ring

Title: Six lakh of bills from a nursing home with no registration
Claim notification (exhibit A): A motorcyclist injured when our policyholder's car clipped him in Meerut has claimed ₹6.2 lakh of medical expenses before the claims tribunal, with bills from "Shree Sai Nursing Home". The government hospital's medico-legal record shows he was treated there for a fractured wrist and discharged after two days. The nursing home does not appear in the state register of clinical establishments, and its bill numbers run in sequence with bills filed in two other unrelated claims.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): (Claimant's lawyer) After the government hospital my client was shifted to a private nursing home for proper treatment, surgery and physiotherapy for three weeks. The bills are genuine and proved by the treating doctor's certificate.
Other accounts:
Government hospital medico-legal record (Record or log):
Admitted on the day of the accident with a fracture of the right radius. Closed reduction and plaster cast. Discharged after two days with advice to attend the fracture clinic. No referral to any private facility recorded.

Verification report (Report):
"Shree Sai Nursing Home": not found in the state register of clinical establishments; address is a residential flat. Treating doctor's registration number belongs to a dentist registered in another state. Bill numbers 1187 to 1191 used here; bills 1185 and 1192 filed in two other tribunal claims on different dates.
Damage: Fractured right radius treated with a cast. Claimed medical expenses ₹6.2 lakh; real expenses minimal.
Third parties:
Deepak Chauhan
His lawyer
The purported nursing home and doctor
Evidence:
Government hospital medico-legal record
Verification report on the nursing home and doctor
Bills filed in the tribunal
What happened (answer): A genuine accident and a real wrist fracture treated at a government hospital. The nursing home treatment and bills were fabricated to inflate the claim.
Missing information (answer):
The fracture clinic follow-up records
X-rays from any private facility
Inconsistencies (answer): The lawyer says surgery was done at the nursing home; the government hospital treated the fracture with a cast and recorded no referral
Fraud indicators (answer):
Unregistered facility at a residential address
Doctor's registration belongs to a dentist in another state
Bill numbers shared with other claims
Innocent explanations (answer): A claimant can be misled by a tout who arranges paperwork, but the bills still cannot be paid
Questions to ask (answer):
Put the verification report to the claimant through the tribunal
Ask for the X-rays and implant details of the claimed surgery
Next steps (answer):
Contest the medical expenses before the tribunal with the verification report and the government hospital record
Accept the genuine injury: pay compensation for the wrist fracture on the real medical evidence
Link the two other claims with the same bill series and review them
Report the fabricated bills to the police and the medical council
Assessment (answer): Third-party fraud on the medical expenses; the underlying injury is real. Pay what is genuine and contest the fabricated bills.
Recommended action (answer): Contest the bills with the verification evidence, pay the genuine injury claim, and report the fabrication.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Tribunal rejects the bills and awards ₹85,000 for the fracture
Police raid finds a bill-making racket supplying several lawyers
Tags: fake medical bills, nursing home, clinical establishment registration, MLC, MACT, doctor registration

Title: Sold on stamp paper, then reported stolen
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder reported his Toyota Innova stolen from outside a temple in Guntur and an FIR was registered. FASTag records show the vehicle crossing toll plazas between Guntur and Chennai nine times in the five weeks after the reported theft. Two e-challans for speeding were issued to it in Chennai. A used-car dealer has told the investigator that the policyholder sold the car to a buyer on a stamp-paper agreement four months earlier, with the loan to be cleared later.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): I parked at the temple and when I came out it was gone. I don't know who is driving it. I never sold it, the RC is in my name. Some dealers spread stories. Please settle quickly, the bank is calling me about the loan.
Other accounts:
FASTag and e-challan records (Record or log):
Nine toll crossings between Guntur and Chennai in the five weeks after the reported theft, all on the vehicle's FASTag, which is still recharged from a UPI account. Two speeding e-challans issued in Chennai after the theft date.

Used-car dealer (Witness account):
He sold the Innova through me four months ago to a man from Chennai, on a hundred-rupee stamp paper agreement. The buyer was to pay the balance and clear the loan, then transfer the RC. I heard the buyer stopped paying.
Damage: Claimed theft of an Innova; IDV ₹14,20,000. Vehicle in use in Chennai.
Third parties:
The buyer in Chennai
The used-car dealer
The financing bank
Evidence:
FASTag and e-challan records
Dealer's statement
FIR
What happened (answer): He sold the car informally, the buyer stopped paying, and he reported it stolen to recover the money from the insurer.
Missing information (answer):
The stamp paper agreement
The UPI account holder who recharges the FASTag
Inconsistencies (answer):
He says he never sold the car; the dealer says he sold it four months before the theft
The car has been crossing tolls and collecting challans since it was "stolen"
Fraud indicators (answer):
Vehicle in regular use after the reported theft
FASTag still recharged
Private sale without transfer
Loan pressure
Innocent explanations (answer): A buyer who stops paying can leave a seller desperate, but that is not a theft covered by the policy
Questions to ask (answer):
Ask him directly about the sale and the agreement
Identify the UPI account recharging the FASTag
Next steps (answer):
Put the dealer’s account and the toll records to him and take a written statement
Trace the vehicle through the FASTag and challan data and inform the police
Repudiate the theft claim if the sale is confirmed: there was no theft, and he had parted with the car
Report a false theft claim through the proper channels
Assessment (answer): Potential fraud with strong evidence: the car is being driven openly, and a witness describes a private sale.
Recommended action (answer): Investigate the sale, help the police trace the car, and repudiate if confirmed.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Car traced to the buyer; claim withdrawn
Claim repudiated and FIR closed as false

Title: Surveyor on day 3, report on day 28, no decision on day 48
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder intimated an own-damage claim on 1 July after her car was rear-ended in heavy rain in Pune. Claimant's statement (exhibit B): My car has been sitting at the garage for seven weeks. Every time I call, I'm told the file is under process. I have sent every document they asked for. I'm paying for cabs every day. Isn't there a rule about how long this can take?
Other accounts:
Claim timeline (Record or log):
1 July: claim intimated. 4 July: surveyor appointed. 6 July: survey. 29 July: final survey report received. 1 August: grievance received, no response logged. 18 August: no decision. All documents received by 8 July.

Bima Bharosa complaint notice (Document):
Complaint registered against the insurer for delay in claim settlement. Insurer to resolve and update the portal.
Damage: Her Baleno: rear bumper, boot lid and tail lamps; surveyor's assessment ₹72,000.
Third parties: The driver who rear-ended her
Evidence:
Claim timeline
Bima Bharosa complaint notice
Survey report

Find out why the grievance went unanswered and fix the queue

Settled with interest within 3 days; complaint closed
Review finds 300 monsoon claims past the 7-day decision limit

Title: ₹72,000 cut from a zero-depreciation claim with no explanation
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder's SUV was hit on its side at a junction in Kochi. His policy has a zero-depreciation add-on. The repair bill was ₹2,10,000 and the insurer paid ₹1,38,000. The settlement letter lists three deductions without detail: "depreciation ₹42,000", "not related to accident ₹18,000" and "labour cut ₹12,000". He wrote to the grievance cell 40 days ago and has had no reply. He is preparing a complaint to the Insurance Ombudsman.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): I paid extra every year for zero dep precisely so this wouldn't happen. Nobody has told me what "not related to accident" means. The surveyor saw the car with me. I've written to them, nobody answers. I'll go to the ombudsman if I have to.
Other accounts:
Settlement letter (Document):
Repair invoice ₹2,10,000. Less: depreciation ₹42,000; not related to accident ₹18,000; labour cut ₹12,000. Amount paid ₹1,38,000. Policy add-ons: zero depreciation.

Grievance log (Record or log):
Grievance received 40 days ago asking for a breakdown of the deductions. Status: open, unassigned.
Damage: Mahindra XUV700: front door, rear door, B-pillar trim and side mirror; repair ₹2,10,000.
Third parties: The other driver
Evidence:
Settlement letter
Grievance log
Repair invoice
Survey report
What happened (answer): A genuine claim underpaid. The depreciation deduction ignores his zero-depreciation add-on, and the other deductions were never explained.
Missing information (answer): The surveyor's working for the ₹18,000 and the labour cut
Inconsistencies (answer): Depreciation deducted on a policy with a zero-depreciation add-on

Next steps (answer):
Refund the ₹42,000 depreciation: the zero-depreciation add-on covers it
Review the other deductions against the survey report and give a written, item-by-item explanation; refund any not supported
Answer his grievance in writing now
Explain his right to approach the Insurance Ombudsman within a year of the insurer’s reply (or one month without a reply) for claims up to ₹50 lakh, and expect the deductions to be scrutinised there
Assessment (answer): Genuine and underpaid, with unexplained deductions and an ignored grievance. A clear ombudsman risk the insurer should fix itself.
Recommended action (answer): Refund the depreciation, justify or refund the other deductions, and answer the grievance in writing.
Possible outcomes (answer):
₹54,000 refunded with an item-wise explanation; ombudsman complaint not filed
Ombudsman awards the full difference

Title: A thumbprint on "full and final" at the garage counter
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder, aged 64, from a village near Gaya, Bihar, owns a car driven by her son for the family business. After it hit a tree, the surveyor assessed the loss at ₹1,10,000 and the garage bill came to ₹1,08,000. At the garage, the surveyor gave her a discharge voucher for ₹62,000 marked "full and final" and told her she would not get the car back unless she signed. She cannot read English and put her thumbprint on it. She now wants the balance.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): (Through her son) The sahib said sign here or the car stays here. I don't read English. I thought it was the paper to take the car home. When the money came it was only sixty-two thousand. The garage took the rest from my son.
Other accounts:
Surveyor’s final report extract (Report):
Assessed loss ₹1,10,000 net of depreciation and excess. Recommended for settlement.

Discharge voucher (Document):
"I accept ₹62,000 in full and final settlement of all claims under the policy." Thumb impression of the insured. Witness: the surveyor. Printed in English only.
Damage: Maruti Ertiga: front bumper, radiator, bonnet and headlamps. Garage bill ₹1,08,000; surveyor assessment ₹1,10,000.
Third parties:
The surveyor
The garage
Evidence:
Surveyor's final report
Discharge voucher
Garage bill
Son's account
What happened (answer): A genuine claim underpaid by ₹48,000 through a voucher obtained from an elderly customer who could not read it, under pressure.
Missing information (answer): Why the voucher amount differs from the surveyor’s own assessment
Inconsistencies (answer): The surveyor assessed ₹1,10,000 but witnessed a voucher for ₹62,000

Next steps (answer):
Do not rely on the voucher: a discharge signed under pressure by a customer who could not read it does not prevent her claiming the balance, and forums treat such vouchers sceptically
Pay the balance of the assessed loss with interest for the delay
Investigate the surveyor’s conduct and report it if confirmed
Communicate with her in Hindi, through her son if she wishes, and check whether other customers were treated the same way
Assessment (answer): Genuine claim and a vulnerable customer who was pressured into an unfair discharge. The insurer should correct it before a consumer forum does.
Recommended action (answer): Pay the ₹48,000 balance with interest and investigate the surveyor.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Balance paid; surveyor removed from the panel
Review finds three more vouchers obtained the same way
Tags: discharge voucher, full and final, coercion, vulnerable customer, surveyor conduct, consumer forum

Title: Details swapped on a Brampton street, and no report to the collision centre
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder and another driver collided at a residential intersection in Brampton, Ontario, on an icy evening. They exchanged names and phone numbers and drove away. Neither reported the collision to the police or a collision reporting centre, although the combined damage is clearly over $2,000. Three weeks later he made a claim. The other driver now says the policyholder slid into her and that she will claim against him.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): We were both shaken and it was getting dark, so we took photos of each other's licences and left. I didn't know we had to go to the reporting centre. She was the one who slid through the stop sign, I was already in the intersection. Now she's changing her story.
Other accounts:
Photos taken at the scene (Record or log):
Six photos time-stamped at the scene: both cars at the intersection, the other car's front bumper against the policyholder's rear passenger door, the other driver's licence, and the stop sign on her side of the intersection.

Other driver, through her insurer (Statement):
He came through the intersection too fast for the ice and slid into the front of my car. I had stopped at my sign. I will be making a claim.
Damage: His Civic: rear passenger door and quarter panel, $4,100. Her car: front bumper and headlamp, about $2,300.
Third parties: The other driver and her insurer
Evidence:
Time-stamped scene photos
Other driver's statement through her insurer
Repair estimate
What happened (answer): A genuine collision that should have been reported within 24 hours. The photos are the strongest evidence of where each car was.
Missing information (answer):
A collision report
Any doorbell or dashcam footage from nearby houses
Inconsistencies (answer): Each driver says the other slid into them
Innocent explanations (answer): Many drivers do not know that a collision with over $2,000 of damage must be reported
Questions to ask (answer):
Ask both drivers to report the collision now at a collision reporting centre
Ask neighbours on the intersection for doorbell footage
Next steps (answer):
Ask him to report the collision now; late reporting is a legal issue, not a bar to his claim
Use the photo of the impact point: her bumper against his rear door is consistent with her car striking his side, which supports his account
Apply Ontario’s Fault Determination Rules to the positions and the stop sign, and handle his damage under the coverages on his policy
Respond to her claim through her insurer using the same evidence
Assessment (answer): Genuine collision, not reported as required. The photos support his account; the reporting failure weakens the evidence but does not defeat the claim.
Recommended action (answer): Have the collision reported now, decide fault on the photos and the rules, and handle both claims.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Fault assigned to the other driver under the rules; claim paid
Doorbell footage confirms she rolled through the stop sign
Tags: Ontario, collision reporting centre, $2,000 threshold, late reporting, Fault Determination Rules, denial by other driver

Title: A two-year-old leased SUV, valued as if it were used

Endorsement: removing depreciation deduction, leased vehicle. Vehicle leased new 20 months before the loss. Lessor shown as loss payee.

Settlement offer (Document):
Actual cash value from comparable listings: $41,000, less deductible. Endorsement not referred to.
