Third parties:
The leasing company (lessor and loss payee)
The other drivers
Evidence:
Policy declarations with the endorsement
Lease agreement and original price
Settlement offer
What happened (answer): A genuine total loss within the endorsement period. The offer applied ordinary actual cash value and ignored the endorsement she paid for.
Missing information (answer): The lessor's payout statement
Inconsistencies (answer): The policy carries the endorsement; the offer ignores it
Innocent explanations (answer): The total loss system may not pick up endorsements automatically
Questions to ask (answer): Ask the leasing company for its payout figure
Next steps (answer):
Settle under the endorsement terms instead of actual cash value, since the loss is within the endorsement period
Pay the lessor as loss payee first, then any balance to her
Explain the calculation in writing and apologize for the first offer
Check other recent total losses for the same omission
Assessment (answer): Genuine and covered on better terms than offered. The endorsement she paid for applies.
Recommended action (answer): Re-settle under the removing depreciation endorsement and pay the lessor and her accordingly.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Re-settled at the original price; lessor paid and balance to her
Review finds four other files with the same error
Tags: Ontario, removing depreciation endorsement, leased vehicle, lessor, total loss, loss payee

Title: Hit by a red-light runner in Kelowna, and told she cannot sue him
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder was injured in Kelowna, British Columbia, when another driver ran a red light and hit her car. She has a fractured collarbone and cannot work as a dental hygienist for at least ten weeks. A friend in Alberta told her to hire a lawyer and sue the other driver for pain and suffering. She has asked her insurer why the claim is being handled through accident benefits only.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): He ran the red light, there's a witness and the police ticketed him. Why should I just get benefits? My friend in Calgary got a big settlement for less than this. I want him to pay for what he did to me.
Other accounts:
Police report extract (Report):
Vehicle 2 entered the intersection against a red light and struck vehicle 1. Driver of vehicle 2 issued a violation ticket. Independent witness statement attached.

Benefits summary (Document):
Accident occurred after May 2021: Enhanced Care benefits apply. Medical and rehabilitation benefits, income replacement at 90% of net income up to the statutory maximum, and a permanent impairment benefit if applicable.
Damage: Fractured collarbone, ten weeks off work. Car: front-left damage.
Third parties:
The red-light driver
Independent witness
Evidence:
Police report with the ticket
Witness statement
Medical records
Employer letter on earnings
What happened (answer): A genuine not-at-fault injury in British Columbia, where the Enhanced Care model replaced most lawsuits for injuries with care-based benefits.
Missing information (answer): Her pay records for the income replacement calculation
Innocent explanations (answer): Rules differ sharply between provinces, and advice from Alberta does not apply in BC
Questions to ask (answer): Ask for her pay records and her physiotherapy plan
Next steps (answer):
Explain that in BC, for accidents since May 2021, the right to sue an at-fault driver for injuries has been removed in most cases and replaced by care-based benefits
Pay her benefits promptly: treatment, income replacement and any impairment benefit
Tell her how to request a review if she disagrees with a benefit decision
Record the other driver as at fault for her vehicle damage and premium purposes
Assessment (answer): Genuine and covered under Enhanced Care benefits. Her wish to sue is understandable but generally not available in BC.
Recommended action (answer): Explain the model clearly, pay all benefits she is entitled to, and set out the review route.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Benefits paid; she returns to work after 11 weeks
Review request on income replacement partly upheld
Tags: British Columbia, Enhanced Care, no-fault, right to sue, care-based benefits, income replacement

Title: Changing lanes on the Queensway, rated 100% at fault
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder was changing lanes on the Queensway in Ottawa when a car in the next lane hit his rear quarter. Under Ontario's Fault Determination Rules for a lane change, he has been rated 100% at fault, which will affect his premium. He says the other driver sped up to close the gap. He complained to the insurer, was unhappy with the reply, and asked how to take it further.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): I signalled for five seconds, there was a big gap. He saw me and floored it to stop me getting in. The dashcam shows him speeding up. How can a rule say I'm 100% at fault when he did it on purpose?
Other accounts:
Policyholder’s dashcam (rear-facing) (Record or log):
Indicator on for about five seconds before the lane change. The following car's headlights grow quickly in the frame in the last two seconds, consistent with it accelerating. Contact at the rear quarter as the lane change completes.

First complaint response (Document):
Fault has been determined under Ontario Regulation 668, the Fault Determination Rules. A vehicle changing lanes that collides with a vehicle in the other lane is 100% at fault. We cannot change this determination.
Damage: His Camry: rear quarter and bumper, $3,300. Other car: front corner.
Third parties: The other driver and their insurer
Evidence:
Rear-facing dashcam
First complaint response
What happened (answer): A lane-change collision where the other driver probably accelerated to block him. The Fault Determination Rules still put the lane-changing driver at fault for rating and direct compensation purposes.
Missing information (answer): Any witness who saw the other car accelerate
Inconsistencies (answer): He says the other driver accelerated deliberately; the rules take no account of that
Innocent explanations (answer): Customers reasonably expect fault to reflect what actually happened
Questions to ask (answer): Ask whether he wants to report the other driver’s conduct to the police
Next steps (answer):
Explain clearly and without jargon that the Fault Determination Rules apply as written for rating and his own damage, whatever the other driver’s conduct
Note that the rules do not decide fault in a lawsuit, and that dangerous driving can be reported to the police
Escalate his complaint to the insurer’s internal ombudsman if he remains unhappy, and then explain his right to go to the General Insurance OmbudService and the regulator
Keep the dashcam on file in case it becomes relevant to any injury claim
Assessment (answer): Genuinely disputed in fairness, but the rule is applied correctly. Good handling means a clear explanation and an open path for his complaint.
Recommended action (answer): Maintain the rule-based determination, explain it plainly, and guide him through the escalation route.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Complaint closed after the internal ombudsman explains the rules
General Insurance OmbudService finds the rules were applied correctly
Tags: Ontario, Fault Determination Rules, lane change, complaint, General Insurance OmbudService, premium impact

Title: Bought on Marketplace, insured for four months, stolen all along
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder bought a two-year-old Toyota Highlander through an online marketplace in Laval, Quebec, for $38,000 in cash, and insured it. Four months later he rear-ended a car on an icy road and claimed for both. The appraiser noticed the public VIN plate had been re-riveted. A check of the hidden secondary VIN shows the vehicle was stolen in Mississauga, Ontario, five months before he bought it. The VIN on his paperwork belongs to a Highlander that was written off in Alberta.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): The seller met me at a mall, showed me the registration and a clean history report for the VIN. I paid cash because he said the bank transfer would take days. I had no idea. I've lost $38,000 and now you're telling me the car isn't even mine.
Other accounts:
Appraiser’s report (Report):
Public VIN plate shows non-factory rivets. Secondary VIN read from a concealed location does not match. Secondary VIN reported stolen in Ontario five months before the purchase. Public VIN belongs to a vehicle recorded as a total loss in Alberta.

Purchase documents (Document):
Handwritten bill of sale, $38,000 cash. Copy of a registration in the seller's name bearing the cloned VIN. Vehicle history report for the cloned VIN, showing no accidents.
Damage: Highlander: front end, $7,800. Other car: rear bumper and trunk, $4,200.
Third parties:
The driver he rear-ended
The original owner and their insurer
The seller
Evidence:
Appraiser's report
Purchase documents
Stolen vehicle record
What happened (answer): He is the victim of a re-VINning scheme: he bought a stolen vehicle disguised with the identity of a written-off car.
Missing information (answer):
The seller’s real identity
The original owner’s insurer and whether it paid a theft claim
Inconsistencies (answer): The paperwork VIN belongs to a written-off vehicle; the hidden VIN belongs to a stolen one
Fraud indicators (answer):
Re-riveted VIN plate
Cash sale in a mall car park
History report run on the cloned VIN
Innocent explanations (answer): Clean history reports on a cloned VIN fool many buyers
Questions to ask (answer):
Ask for any messages with the seller and the listing
Identify the original owner’s insurer
Next steps (answer):
Treat the policyholder as a fraud victim and help him report to the police
Notify the police and the original owner’s insurer; the vehicle belongs to the original owner or to the insurer that paid its theft claim
Get advice on the third party’s claim: he was insured as the driver of that vehicle, and the person he hit should not be left without a remedy
Decline the own-damage claim, since he has no ownership interest in the stolen vehicle, and refund the premium for the vehicle cover
Assessment (answer): The policyholder is genuine and a victim; the vehicle is stolen. Ownership, not his honesty, decides the own-damage claim.
Recommended action (answer): Report the stolen vehicle, deal fairly with the third party, decline own damage and refund the premium.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Vehicle returned to the original owner’s insurer; third party paid; premium refunded
Police link the seller to a ring that re-VINned 40 vehicles
Tags: re-VIN, cloned VIN, stolen vehicle, innocent buyer, marketplace sale, ownership

Title: The other driver gave a name, a number, and a car he no longer owned
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder has a third party property policy with an uninsured motorist extension, which pays up to $5,000 for her car's damage if an identified, uninsured driver is at fault. Her car was rear-ended at lights in Brisbane in heavy rain. The other driver gave a name and mobile number, which no longer answers. The plate she photographed is registered to a woman who says she sold the car two months ago and the buyer never transferred the registration.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): He was really apologetic, he said he had no insurance and would pay me himself. I took a photo of his plate and his car. Now his number's dead. The repair quote is $6,800. I only have third party cover because I can't afford comprehensive.
Other accounts:
Registered operator (Statement):
I sold that car on an online marketplace two months ago for cash. I filled in my half of the transfer form and gave the buyer the rest. He obviously never lodged it. I have a screenshot of our messages and his first name.

Policy extension wording (Document):
Uninsured motorist extension: we pay up to $5,000 for damage to your car if the other driver was at fault, did not have insurance, and you can give us their name and address or the vehicle's registration details.
Damage: Her Mazda 3: rear bumper, boot and tail lamps, quote $6,800.
Third parties:
The unidentified at-fault driver
The registered operator who sold the car
Evidence:
Photo of the other car and its plate
Registered operator's statement and sale messages
Repair quote
Policy extension wording
What happened (answer): A genuine rear-end collision by an uninsured driver. The extension may apply, but the at-fault driver's identity is not yet established.
Missing information (answer):
The buyer’s full name and address
A police report
Innocent explanations (answer): Unlodged registration transfers after private sales are common
Questions to ask (answer):
Ask the registered operator for the buyer’s messages and payment details
Ask the policyholder to report the collision to the police
Next steps (answer):
Check the wording: the extension can be met with the vehicle’s registration details and evidence the driver was at fault and uninsured
Help identify the buyer through the sale messages and a police report
If the conditions are met, pay up to the $5,000 limit; explain that the rest can only be pursued against the driver
Keep her informed while the identification is attempted
Assessment (answer): Insufficient evidence for now, with a genuine policyholder. The registration and photo may be enough under the wording; identifying the buyer would settle it.
Recommended action (answer): Pursue the buyer's identity, assess the extension on the registration evidence, and pay up to the limit if met.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Buyer identified through the sale messages; $5,000 paid and recovery pursued
Paid on the registration evidence alone under the wording
Tags: third party property, uninsured motorist extension, at-fault driver details, registration transfer, Queensland, limit

Title: Lodged in February, still undecided in June
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder lodged a comprehensive claim on 3 February after his parked car was hit in a shopping centre car park in Adelaide. An assessor was appointed but he was not told for three weeks. He received no updates for nine weeks. He complained on 1 June and has had no response. On 20 June, more than four months after lodgement, there is no decision and no exceptional circumstances are recorded.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): It's a straightforward scrape, the centre's CCTV shows the other car. I've rung every fortnight and I'm told it's with the assessor. I complained in writing three weeks ago and heard nothing. I've been driving around with a door held shut with tape.
Other accounts:
Claim timeline (Record or log):
3 Feb: claim lodged. 10 Feb: assessor appointed; customer told 3 Mar. Assessor report received 28 Mar. No customer update between 3 Mar and 5 May. 1 Jun: written complaint received, not acknowledged. 20 Jun: no decision. Exceptional circumstances: none recorded.

Shopping centre CCTV request (Record or log):
Footage supplied 14 Feb showing a white ute reversing into the policyholder's car and leaving. Plate partly legible.
Damage: His Corolla: driver's door and rear door dented; door does not close; quote $3,400.
Third parties: Driver of the white ute
Evidence:
Claim timeline
CCTV footage
Assessor's report
What happened (answer): A straightforward claim left without a decision, updates or a complaint response, in breach of the Code's timeframes.
Missing information (answer): The reason no decision was made after the assessor’s report
Innocent explanations (answer): Assessor backlogs after storms delay many claims, but the Code still applies
Questions to ask (answer): Check whether the ute driver can be identified from the partial plate for recovery
Next steps (answer):
Decide the claim now: all the information has been on file since late March
Record the Code breaches: late notice of the assessor, no updates at least every 20 business days, no decision within 10 business days of having the information or within 4 months
Respond to the complaint in writing within the Code’s complaint timeframe, and tell him he can take it to AFCA if unhappy
Consider compensation for the delay and fix the update process
Assessment (answer): Genuine and overdue. The insurer has breached several Code timeframes and should decide, apologize and explain the AFCA route.
Recommended action (answer): Approve the claim now, respond to the complaint with the AFCA option, and address the delay.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Claim approved the same week; complaint closed with a goodwill payment
AFCA complaint finds the delays unreasonable
Tags: General Insurance Code of Practice, 4 months, 20 business days, complaint, AFCA, assessor

Title: Her ex-partner smashed the car, and he is still on the policy
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder holds a comprehensive policy on which her former partner is still listed as a named driver and joint policyholder. After they separated, he smashed the windscreen and lights and scratched the panels of the car outside her home in Geelong. Police attended and a family violence intervention order is now in place. She has claimed for the damage. The claims team has flagged the policy's exclusion for damage caused intentionally by "you or anyone acting with your consent".
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): I just need the car fixed so I can get the kids to school. I didn't know he was still on the policy, we set it up together years ago. Please don't contact him about this. He doesn't know where I'm staying some nights.
Other accounts:
Police report extract (Report):
Attended a family violence incident. Respondent damaged the protected person's vehicle with a steering lock: windscreen, headlights and both doors damaged. Intervention order applied for and granted. Respondent charged with criminal damage.

Policy record (Record or log):
Joint policyholders: Sarah Mitchell and Jason Mitchell. Premiums paid from her account for the last two years. Exclusion: loss or damage caused intentionally by you or a person acting with your express or implied consent.
Damage: Kia Cerato: windscreen, headlights, scratched doors and panels; quote $5,900.
Third parties: Jason Mitchell, the former partner and respondent
Evidence:
Police report and intervention order
Policy record
Repair quote
Photos
What happened (answer): The damage was deliberate family violence by her former partner. She did not cause or consent to it.
Missing information (answer): Her preferred safe contact method
Innocent explanations (answer): Joint policies set up during a relationship are often never updated after separation
Questions to ask (answer): Ask her how and when it is safe to contact her
Next steps (answer):
Apply the insurer’s family violence policy under the Code: do not apply the intentional damage exclusion against a victim who did not cause or consent to the damage
Pay her claim without contacting the former partner or disclosing her details or location to him
Remove him from the policy at her request and update her contact details securely
Offer support referrals, flexible payment of any excess, and a single contact who knows her situation
Assessment (answer): Genuine, and a customer experiencing family violence. The exclusion should not be used against the victim; safety and discretion come first.
Recommended action (answer): Pay the claim, keep her details from the perpetrator, and remove him from the policy.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Claim paid in a week; former partner removed from the policy
Insurer pursues recovery from him through the courts without involving her
Tags: family violence, co-insured, intentional damage exclusion, protection order, safety, Code of Practice

Title: A cash offer at the insurer’s rates, and a quote that includes old hail
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder reversed into a concrete pole in a Perth car park, damaging his rear bumper and tailgate. He asked for a cash settlement. The insurer offered $4,200, based on its preferred repairer's rates. His own repairer quoted $7,900. That quote includes paintless dent repair across the roof and bonnet, and the assessor's photos show hail dents that match a storm two years ago, which he never claimed.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): My repairer is who I trust, and he says $4,200 won't cover it. Your repairers get discounts I can't get. I don't see why I should be out of pocket. The hail dents were always there, I just thought they'd do them while it was in.
Other accounts:
Assessor’s comparison (Report):
Collision damage: rear bumper, tailgate, reversing sensor. Customer's quote includes $2,600 of roof and bonnet dent repair for hail damage not related to this incident. Insurer's offer uses preferred repairer labour rates about 20% below the customer's repairer.

Weather record (Record or log):
Hailstorm over the policyholder's suburb two years before this claim. No hail claim lodged on this policy.
Damage: Rear bumper, tailgate and reversing sensor. Separate old hail dents on the roof and bonnet.
Third parties: None
Evidence:
Assessor's comparison
Customer's repairer quote
Weather record
Photos
What happened (answer): A genuine collision. The customer's quote adds unrelated hail damage, while the insurer's offer uses discounted rates he cannot get.
Missing information (answer): A breakdown of the insurer’s offer that the customer can check
Inconsistencies (answer): His quote presents hail repairs as part of this claim
Fraud indicators (answer): Unrelated damage added to the repair quote
Innocent explanations (answer): Customers often ask repairers to fix everything at once without thinking about what the claim covers
Questions to ask (answer): Ask his repairer to requote for the collision damage only
Next steps (answer):
Remove the hail repairs from the quote: they are unrelated and were never claimed
Make a fair cash settlement for the collision damage that reflects what it would reasonably cost him, not only the insurer’s discounted rates, and explain how it was worked out
Give him the itemised breakdown and the option of a repair through the insurer instead of cash
Tell him he can lodge a separate hail claim if within the policy terms, or arrange that repair himself
Assessment (answer): Mixed. The hail damage should come out, but a cash offer at internal discount rates is not fair either.
Recommended action (answer): Exclude the hail items, recalculate a fair cash figure, and explain it with an itemised breakdown.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Cash settled at $5,050 after a collision-only requote
Customer chooses an insurer-arranged repair instead
Tags: cash settlement, preferred repairer rates, pre-existing hail, quote comparison, fairness, Code of Practice

Title: "Free hail repair, no excess", from a pop-up in the car park
Claim notification (exhibit A): After a hailstorm in Melbourne's north, a repair business set up in a shopping centre car park offering "free hail repair, no excess". It lodged a claim on the policyholder's behalf under a signed authority, with an estimate of $11,400. The assessor found light hail dents on the roof, but the estimate also includes old door dings and a cracked bumper. Forty claims from the same business show near-identical estimates, and six of the cars are registered to addresses outside the hail zone.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): They said my insurance would cover it all and I wouldn't pay a cent. I signed their form on an iPad. I didn't know they'd put in the bumper, that crack's been there since my son reversed into the letterbox.
Other accounts:
Assessor’s inspection (Report):
Light hail damage to the roof and bonnet consistent with the storm, fairly priced at about $3,200. Estimate also claims door dings with old paint wear and a cracked bumper with dirt in the crack. Dent repair rates in the estimate about double the local market.

Claims analytics note (Report):
Forty claims from the same business in two weeks. Estimate wording and line items near-identical. Six vehicles registered to suburbs outside the storm footprint. Excess "waived" by the business on every claim.
Damage: Light hail dents to the roof and bonnet. Old door dings and a cracked bumper not caused by hail.
Third parties: The pop-up hail repair business
Evidence:
Assessor's inspection
Claims analytics note
The signed authority
The estimate
What happened (answer): The policyholder has genuine light hail damage. The repair business inflated the estimate with old damage and inflated rates, and is doing so across many claims.
Missing information (answer): Where the six out-of-area cars actually were during the storm
Inconsistencies (answer): The estimate attributes old door dings and a cracked bumper to hail
Fraud indicators (answer):
Excess waived as a sales offer
Near-identical estimates across forty claims
Cars outside the storm footprint
Rates double the market
Innocent explanations (answer): Customers sign authorities quickly when promised a free repair
Questions to ask (answer):
Ask the policyholder whether she understood what the form allowed the business to do
Ask the six out-of-area owners where their cars were parked
Next steps (answer):
Pay the genuine hail damage at a fair rate, directly or through a repairer she chooses, and tell her what was excluded and why
Explain her excess remains payable under her policy; a waiver offered by the business does not change it
Refer the business’s claims as a group to the fraud team and review all forty
Report the conduct to the regulator if the investigation supports it
Assessment (answer): Potential fraud by the repairer, not the customer. Pay her genuine hail damage and investigate the business across all its claims.
Recommended action (answer): Pay the fair hail cost, decline the old damage, and investigate the business's forty claims together.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Business’s claims reduced across the portfolio; two referred to police
Customer chooses her own repairer for the hail work
Tags: hail, pop-up repairer, authority to act, excess waiver, inflated estimate, pre-existing damage

Title: A Patrol on the dunes near Al Faqa, and no off-road extension
Accident type: Single vehicle or loss of control
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder rolled his Nissan Patrol onto its roof while driving over dunes near Al Faqa on a weekend trip with friends. Nobody was hurt. A friend's 4x4 pulled the car back onto its wheels and a recovery truck took it to Dubai. His comprehensive policy excludes use off paved roads unless the optional off-road extension is bought, and it was not bought.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): Everyone goes to the dunes at the weekend, the car is built for it. I went over a crest a bit fast and the sand gave way. I thought comprehensive meant everything. The salesman never mentioned off-road. The roof is crushed and the pillars are bent.
Other accounts:
Police report extract (Report):
Single vehicle overturned in a desert area off the paved road near Al Faqa. No injuries. No third party involved. Driver licensed.

Policy wording (Document):
Exclusion: loss or damage while the vehicle is being driven off paved roads, including desert and dune driving, unless the off-road extension is shown in the schedule. Schedule: off-road extension not purchased.
Damage: Patrol: roof crushed, A and B pillars bent, windscreen and side glass broken; likely a total loss.
Third parties: None
Evidence:
Police report
Policy wording and schedule
Photos
What happened (answer): A genuine rollover during dune driving, which the policy clearly excludes without the extension he did not buy.
Missing information (answer): Sales records showing whether the off-road extension was offered
Innocent explanations (answer): Many buyers assume comprehensive cover includes dune driving
Questions to ask (answer): Ask for the sales call recording or quote to see whether the extension was offered
Next steps (answer):
Decline the own-damage claim under the off-road exclusion, explaining the wording and the extension in plain language
Check the sales records: if the extension was never offered or explained, handle it as a complaint about the sale
Offer to add the extension at renewal
Assessment (answer): Genuine accident, not covered. The exclusion is clear and the extension was not bought.
Recommended action (answer): Decline with a clear explanation and review how the policy was sold.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Declined; he accepts after the wording is explained
Complaint about the sale upheld; goodwill contribution offered
Tags: dune driving, off-road exclusion, off-road extension, rollover, desert, policy wording

Title: Found scraped in the Marina car park, reported four days later
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder says he found a long scrape and dent on his car's rear quarter when he returned to it in a residential car park in Dubai Marina. He obtained a police report for damage by an unknown party four days later, because he was travelling for work. The garage needs the police report to repair the car. The building's CCTV is kept for only three days and has been overwritten.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): I came back late, saw the scrape in the morning and had to fly to Riyadh the same day. I did the police report as soon as I landed back. It's a residents' car park, someone must have scraped it parking. There's yellow paint in the scratch.
Other accounts:
Police report (Report):
Report of damage to a parked vehicle by an unknown party, registered four days after the stated date of discovery. Location: residential building car park, Dubai Marina. No witnesses identified.

Building management (Record or log):
CCTV retention is 72 hours. Footage for the date given has been overwritten. Car park access logs show the policyholder's tag entering the night before and leaving the following morning.
Damage: Lexus IS: rear quarter scrape and dent with yellow paint transfer; estimate AED 4,800.
Third parties: Unknown driver
Evidence:
Police report
Access logs
Photos showing yellow paint transfer
What happened (answer): Probably genuine car park damage by an unknown driver, but the four-day gap means the CCTV is gone and the timing cannot be confirmed.
Missing information (answer):
CCTV of the incident
Whether any resident in the building drives a yellow car
Fraud indicators (answer): Damage reported to police four days after discovery
Innocent explanations (answer): Work travel explains the delay, and the access log supports his movements
Questions to ask (answer):
Ask building management whether any yellow vehicle is registered to the car park
Ask for his flight booking to confirm the travel
Next steps (answer):
Accept the police report as meeting the requirement for repair, and note the reason for the delay
Check the damage height and the yellow paint against the car park, for example yellow-painted pillars or barriers
If consistent, pay the claim as unknown-party damage under the comprehensive cover, applying any excess the policy sets for unknown third parties
Explain that reporting promptly preserves CCTV in future
Assessment (answer): Insufficient evidence rather than suspicion. The travel and the access log support his account; the damage pattern can be checked against the car park.
Recommended action (answer): Inspect the paint transfer against the car park and pay as unknown-party damage if consistent.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Yellow paint matches a column guard near his bay; claim paid
Paid after his flight booking confirms the trip
Tags: unknown party, police report, late report, car park, paint transfer, parking records

Title: Agency repair until three years old, and the car is three years and two months
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder's Lexus ES was rear-ended at a signal in Abu Dhabi; the other driver was found at fault but she has claimed under her own comprehensive policy for speed. The claims team approved repair at a non-agency garage because the car is now three years and two months old and agency repair is "for vehicles up to three years". Her renewal schedule, issued two months before the accident, lists "Agency repair: Yes" for the policy year without any age condition.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): I renewed two months ago and the schedule says agency repair. Nobody told me it would stop halfway through the year. The car has always been serviced at the agency. I want it repaired there with genuine parts, that's what I paid for.
Other accounts:
Renewal schedule (Document):
Period of insurance: 12 months from renewal. Repair condition: Agency repair: Yes. No age limit stated in the schedule.

Claims team note (Record or log):
Vehicle first registered 3 years 2 months before the accident. Underwriting guideline: agency repair up to 3 years. Approved non-agency repair.
Damage: Lexus ES: rear bumper, boot lid and parking sensors; agency estimate AED 9,600, non-agency estimate AED 6,900.
Third parties: The at-fault driver and their insurer
Evidence:
Renewal schedule
Claims team note
Police report finding the other driver at fault
Both estimates
What happened (answer): A genuine claim where the internal guideline conflicts with the schedule the customer was given, which grants agency repair for the whole year.
Missing information (answer): Any wording elsewhere in the policy that limits agency repair by age
Inconsistencies (answer): The schedule grants agency repair without an age limit; the internal guideline sets one
Innocent explanations (answer): Underwriting guidelines are not always reflected in the documents issued to customers
Questions to ask (answer): Check the full policy wording for any age condition on agency repair
Next steps (answer):
Honour agency repair for this policy period: the schedule issued to her grants it without an age condition, and an internal guideline cannot override her contract
Recover the cost from the at-fault driver’s insurer under the police report
Fix the renewal documents so that any age limit is stated clearly at renewal
Assessment (answer): Genuine claim and a fair complaint. The schedule she was given decides the entitlement.
Recommended action (answer): Authorise the agency repair and recover from the at-fault driver's insurer.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Agency repair authorised; full recovery from the other insurer
Renewal schedules updated to show age limits
Tags: agency repair, vehicle age, policy schedule, renewal, non-agency garage, policy period

Title: A tourist in a rental car, a police report, and an insurer that will not pay
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder's car was hit at a roundabout in Abu Dhabi by a rental car driven by a visiting tourist. The police report found the tourist at fault for entering without giving way. The insurer paid her repairs of AED 14,500 under her comprehensive cover and claimed the amount from the rental car's insurer. That insurer has refused, saying the tourist emailed after leaving the country to say she was not at fault.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): The police came, looked at both cars and the position, and gave her the fault. She signed the report too. I don't understand how an email from abroad can change that.
Other accounts:
Police report (Report):
Collision at a roundabout. Vehicle 2 (rental, driven by a visitor) entered without giving way to vehicle 1 already on the roundabout. Fault: vehicle 2. Both drivers signed.

Rental car insurer’s reply (Document):
Our insured's driver disputes liability by email and has left the UAE. We are unable to accept the claim at this time.
Damage: Policyholder's Accord: front-right wing and bumper, AED 14,500, repaired.
Third parties:
The tourist driver
The rental company and its insurer
Evidence:
Signed police report
Rental insurer's refusal
Repair invoice
What happened (answer): A collision caused by the tourist, recorded in a signed police report. Her later email does not change the report.
Missing information (answer): Any formal objection to the police report filed by the tourist
Inconsistencies (answer): The tourist signed the report but now disputes fault by email
Innocent explanations (answer): Visitors sometimes sign reports they do not fully understand
Questions to ask (answer): Ask the rental insurer whether any formal objection to the police report was lodged
Next steps (answer):
Press the recovery on the police report, which assigned fault and was signed by both drivers
Ask the rental insurer to show any formal objection; an informal email is not one
Escalate through the UAE’s insurance dispute channels if the refusal continues
Recover her excess as part of the claim and keep her informed
Assessment (answer): Disputed only by the other side's informal objection. The signed police report supports full recovery.
Recommended action (answer): Pursue the rental car's insurer on the police report and escalate if it keeps refusing.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Rental insurer pays after escalation
Recovered through the dispute process with costs

Title: Paid on the expert’s report, without the repair, and with VAT
Claim notification (exhibit A): Our policyholder reversed into Ms Krüger's parked car in a supermarket car park in Hanover. Liability is accepted. She has claimed on the basis of her expert's report without having the car repaired: €6,300 net repair costs at brand-workshop rates, plus €1,197 VAT, the expert's fee and a flat sum for expenses. Her car is six years old and has been serviced at independent garages.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): I'll decide later whether to repair it or sell it. The expert's report says €7,497 including VAT, so that's what I'm claiming. Why would I get less than the report says?
Other accounts:
Expert report summary (Report):
Damage to the rear bumper, tailgate and rear panel. Repair costs at brand-workshop rates: €6,300 net, €1,197 VAT, €7,497 gross. Vehicle age 6 years. Service history: independent garages.

Our policyholder (Statement):
I was reversing out of the space and didn't see her car behind me. I accepted it on the spot and gave her my details.
Damage: Her VW Passat: rear bumper, tailgate and rear panel.
Third parties:
Sabine Krüger
Her expert
Evidence:
Expert report
Our policyholder's statement
Expert’s invoice
What happened (answer): A clear liability claim settled on a notional basis. VAT is not payable unless it is actually incurred, and brand-workshop rates may be replaced by a cheaper equivalent workshop for a car of this age and service history.
Missing information (answer): Quotes from an equivalent independent workshop nearby
Innocent explanations (answer): Claimants often expect the gross figure in an expert report to be paid in full
Questions to ask (answer): Confirm whether she has had the car repaired or replaced
Next steps (answer):
Pay the net repair costs: under section 249(2) of the Civil Code, VAT is only payable if it is actually incurred
Consider referring her to an equivalent independent workshop’s rates, since the car is over three years old and not serviced at brand workshops, giving her a concrete, reachable alternative
Pay the expert’s fee and the usual flat sum for expenses
Tell her VAT will be paid if she later repairs and shows the invoice
Assessment (answer): Genuine claim, overstated by the VAT. A notional settlement pays net costs; VAT follows only if incurred.
Recommended action (answer): Pay net repair costs, the expert's fee and the expense sum, and explain the VAT rule.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Net costs paid; VAT paid later on a repair invoice
Settled at independent workshop rates after a concrete referral
Tags: fiktive Abrechnung, notional settlement, VAT, expert report, Section 249 BGB, brand workshop

Title: €612 cut from the workshop invoice, and the 2024 rulings on who bears it
Claim notification (exhibit A): Our policyholder rear-ended Mr Brandt in Stuttgart. He had his car repaired at a workshop of his choice and sent the invoice of €5,940. The claims team paid €5,328, cutting €612 for a "workstation change" charge, extra cleaning and a paint mixing surcharge that its estimating system marks as unnecessary. Mr Brandt has not paid the workshop the balance and the workshop is pressing him.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): I took the car to a proper workshop and paid what I could. I can't check whether a workstation change was needed, I'm not a mechanic. Your insurer caused this, why am I stuck between you and the workshop?
Other accounts:
Workshop invoice extract (Document):
Repair per expert report: €5,328. Additional items: workstation change €227, vehicle cleaning and disinfection €148, paint mixing surcharge €237. Total €5,940.

Claims team note (Record or log):
Paid €5,328. Deducted €612 as not necessary according to the estimating system. No contact with the workshop.
Damage: His Audi A3: rear bumper, boot lid and rear panel, repaired.
Third parties:
Lukas Brandt
The workshop
Evidence:
Workshop invoice
Claims team note
Expert report
What happened (answer): A genuine repair where the insurer cut items the claimant could not reasonably judge. Under the Federal Court of Justice rulings of January 2024, that workshop risk falls on the liable insurer.
Missing information (answer): Whether he has assigned his claim to the workshop
Innocent explanations (answer): Estimating systems flag common surcharges whether or not they were justified on a particular job
Questions to ask (answer): Ask whether he has paid the balance and whether he has assigned his claim to the workshop
Next steps (answer):
Pay the €612: following the Federal Court of Justice rulings of 16 January 2024, the claimant who had the repair done can claim the full invoice even if some items were unnecessary; if he has not paid the workshop, payment goes to the workshop
In return, ask him to assign any claims he has against the workshop for overcharging, and pursue the workshop directly if the items were unjustified
Note that if the workshop itself claims under an assignment from him, it cannot rely on the workshop risk rule
Update the deduction practice for repaired-vehicle claims
Assessment (answer): Genuine, and the deduction is against current case law. The insurer pays and takes over the dispute with the workshop.
Recommended action (answer): Pay the balance to the workshop against an assignment of his claims, and pursue the workshop if warranted.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Balance paid; workshop justifies two of the three items
Practice changed for repaired-vehicle invoices
Tags: Werkstattrisiko, workshop risk, BGH 2024, invoice reduction, assignment of claims, repair costs

Title: Fourteen days of loss of use, and a second car in the garage
Fraud type: False hire, towing or storage costs
Claim notification (exhibit A): Our policyholder hit Mr Wagner's car at a junction in Leipzig; liability is accepted. He did not hire a car during the repair and claims loss of use compensation for 14 days at the table rate for his car's class. The expert estimated 5 working days for the repair. He started the repair nine days after the accident, after a holiday. His wife's Golf was available at home, and he says he used it to get to work.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): I couldn't use my own car for two weeks, so I'm owed for two weeks. Yes, I borrowed my wife's Golf for work, but that's her car, not mine. And the holiday was booked months ago, I couldn't take the car in before.
Other accounts:
Expert report extract (Report):
Repair duration: 5 working days. Vehicle drivable and safe to use until repair, with a damaged front wing and headlamp alignment to be checked.

Workshop record (Record or log):
Vehicle delivered for repair 9 days after the accident. Repair completed in 5 working days.
Damage: His Skoda Octavia: front wing, bumper and headlamp. Drivable.
Third parties: Thomas Wagner
Evidence:
Expert report
Workshop record
His statement about his wife's car
What happened (answer): A genuine claim for loss of use, overstated: the car was drivable before the repair, the necessary repair period was 5 working days, and a second household car was available and used.
Missing information (answer): Whether his wife needed her car during those days
Inconsistencies (answer): He claims 14 days; the car was drivable before the repair and the repair took 5 working days
Fraud indicators (answer): Loss of use claimed for days when the car was drivable and another car was used
Innocent explanations (answer): Many claimants believe loss of use runs from the accident until the car comes back
Questions to ask (answer): Ask whether his wife went without her car during those days
Next steps (answer):
Limit loss of use to the necessary repair period, here about 5 working days, because the car was drivable before
Consider the household second car: if it was genuinely available to him without hardship to others, loss of use may not be due at all; if his wife went without, a payment for the repair days is fair
Explain the calculation clearly and pay the undisputed repair costs
Assessment (answer): Genuine claim, exaggerated in duration. At most the repair days are payable, and the second car may remove the loss entirely.
Recommended action (answer): Pay the repair costs and, depending on the second car's availability, loss of use for the repair days only.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Loss of use paid for 7 calendar days
Loss of use declined because the second car was freely available
Tags: Nutzungsausfall, loss of use, second car, repair duration, mitigation, compensation table

Title: Twenty-six reports by the same expert, all generous
Claim notification (exhibit A): A claimant in Duisburg says our policyholder scraped his rear bumper while parking. His expert's report prices a new bumper, a new rear panel section, blend painting of both rear doors and €900 of diminished value for a nine-year-old car with 180,000 km. The claimant's photos show a scrape on the bumper corner only. The same expert, lawyer and workshop appear in 26 claims against the insurer in nine months, all with similar line items.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): (Lawyer for the claimant) The report is by a certified independent expert and must be paid in full, together with the expert's fee and our fees. Your policyholder admitted fault.
Other accounts:
Claimant’s photos and report (Record or log):
Photos: a 15 cm scrape on the rear bumper corner, no visible deformation of the rear panel. Report: bumper replacement, rear panel section, blend painting of both rear doors, diminished value €900. Total €4,980 net.

Claims analytics note (Report):
26 liability claims in 9 months with the same expert, lawyer and workshop. In 21 of them, blend painting of adjacent panels and diminished value were claimed regardless of vehicle age or mileage. Average report value 2.4 times the insurer's own estimates for similar photos.
Damage: BMW 3 Series: scrape to the rear bumper corner.
Third parties:
Mehmet Yilmaz
His expert
His lawyer
The workshop
Evidence:
Claimant's photos and expert report
Claims analytics note
Our policyholder's admission
What happened (answer): A minor genuine scrape, valued by an expert whose reports consistently inflate repairs and add diminished value where little or none can exist.
Missing information (answer): A physical inspection by an independent expert instructed by the insurer
Inconsistencies (answer):
The report replaces a rear panel the photos show undamaged
Diminished value claimed on a nine-year-old car with 180,000 km
Fraud indicators (answer):
Same expert, lawyer and workshop across 26 claims
Repairs priced well above the visible damage
Diminished value claimed regardless of age and mileage
Innocent explanations (answer): Hidden damage behind a bumper corner is possible, which an inspection would reveal
Questions to ask (answer): Ask to inspect the car before it is repaired
Next steps (answer):
Accept liability for the scrape, but not the report: instruct an independent expert to inspect the car
Pay the reasonable repair costs on the inspection; resist diminished value on a car of this age and mileage unless clearly shown
Review the 26 claims together with the counter-fraud team and consider a complaint to the expert’s certifying body
Do not allege fraud in correspondence before the review is complete
Assessment (answer): Potential fraud by inflation across a series of claims. The scrape is real; the report's scope is not supported by the photos.
Recommended action (answer): Inspect independently, pay the reasonable cost, and review the expert's claims as a group.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Settled at €1,150 after inspection
Expert’s certification withdrawn after the group review
Tags: expert report, inflated repair, diminished value, blend painting, counter-expert, pattern

Title: A cyclist hurt in Lyon, and eight months to make an offer
Claim notification (exhibit A): Our policyholder turned across a cyclist, Ms Fontaine, in Lyon on 10 January. She suffered a fractured tibia and a broken wrist and has had two operations. Her doctors say her condition is not yet consolidated. It is now 25 August and no compensation offer has been sent to her. The file note says the handler was waiting for consolidation before making any offer.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): I've been off work since January. I've had two operations and physiotherapy three times a week. Nobody from the insurance has made me any offer, not even something provisional. My lawyer says there are rules about this.
Other accounts:
Medical certificate (Report):
Fracture of the left tibia with internal fixation, fracture of the right wrist. Second operation in May. Not consolidated; consolidation expected in 6 to 9 months.

Handler’s file note (Record or log):
Liability accepted. Awaiting consolidation before making an offer. Interim payment of €3,000 made in March.
Damage: Fractured tibia and wrist, two operations, off work for over seven months. Bicycle destroyed.
Third parties:
Léa Fontaine
Her lawyer
Evidence:
Medical certificate
Handler's file note
Police report
What happened (answer): A cyclist injured by our policyholder, with liability accepted. The insurer has wrongly waited for consolidation and is close to the legal deadline for an offer.
Missing information (answer):
A medical assessment for a provisional offer
Her loss of earnings documents
Innocent explanations (answer): Waiting for consolidation is a common misunderstanding; the law requires a provisional offer meanwhile
Questions to ask (answer): Ask her lawyer for her earnings documents
Next steps (answer):
Make a provisional offer now: the Code des assurances requires an offer to an injured victim within 8 months of the accident, which falls on 10 September, provisional if the condition is not consolidated
Base it on a medical assessment and her documented losses so far, with further interim payments if needed
Diary the final offer: it must follow within 5 months of the insurer learning of consolidation
Note the sanction: a late or manifestly insufficient offer attracts interest at double the legal rate
Assessment (answer): Genuine and serious, liability accepted. The insurer must make a provisional offer before 10 September rather than wait for consolidation.
Recommended action (answer): Arrange a medical assessment and make a reasoned provisional offer before the 8-month deadline.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Provisional offer made on 5 September; final offer after consolidation
Deadline missed; double interest applied by the court
Tags: Loi Badinter, compensation offer, 8 months, provisional offer, consolidation, penalty interest

Title: Hit by an uninsured driver, with third-party cover only
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder's car was hit at a junction in Marseille by a driver who ran a stop sign. The police identified the other driver and found he had no insurance. Policyholder has third-party-only cover, so his own policy does not pay for his car. He asked his insurer who will pay for the €3,800 of damage.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): The police said he had no insurance at all and they seized his car. I only have third-party cover because my car is old. Surely I'm not the one who has to pay when he broke the law?
Other accounts:
Police report extract (Report):
Vehicle B failed to stop at a stop sign and struck vehicle A. Driver of vehicle B identified; no valid insurance; vehicle impounded. Driver of vehicle A not at fault.

Policy schedule (Document):
Third-party liability (responsabilité civile) only. Legal protection option included.
Damage: His Clio: front-left wing, bumper and headlamp, €3,800.
Third parties:
The uninsured driver
The guarantee fund (FGAO)
Evidence:
Police report
Policy schedule
Repair estimate
What happened (answer): A not-at-fault collision with an identified, uninsured driver. His own third-party policy does not cover his car; the national guarantee fund compensates victims of uninsured drivers.
Missing information (answer): The guarantee fund claim form
Innocent explanations (answer): Owners of older cars often choose third-party cover without realising it leaves them exposed to uninsured drivers
Questions to ask (answer): Confirm whether he has started a claim with the guarantee fund
Next steps (answer):
Explain that his third-party policy does not pay for his own car
Guide him to claim from the guarantee fund for victims of uninsured drivers (FGAO), within its time limits and subject to its own conditions and any deductible
Use his legal protection option to help him with the guarantee fund claim and any action against the driver
Record that he was not at fault so his bonus is not affected
Assessment (answer): Genuine and not at fault. The remedy is the guarantee fund, with help from his legal protection cover.
Recommended action (answer): Explain the position, help him claim from the FGAO, and protect his bonus.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Paid by the guarantee fund less its deductible
Legal protection recovers the deductible from the driver
Tags: uninsured driver, FGAO, guarantee fund, third-party only, legal protection, police report

Title: Declared twelve days late because of a funeral abroad
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder had a low-speed collision in a Toulouse car park and completed a joint accident report (constat amiable) with the other driver at the scene. She flew to Algeria the next day for a family funeral and declared the claim to her insurer twelve days after the accident. The claims clerk has proposed refusing the claim for late declaration.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): My uncle died and I left the next morning. I had the constat in my bag the whole time. I declared it the day after I got back. Nothing has changed, the other driver signed everything, and my car hasn't been repaired.
Other accounts:
Constat amiable (Document):
Signed by both drivers at the scene. Vehicle B reversing from a space into vehicle A which was passing behind. Both drivers' insurers and details complete.

Claims clerk note (Record or log):
Declaration received 12 days after the accident; contract requires 5 working days. Propose refusal for late declaration (déchéance).
Damage: Her Peugeot 208: rear door and wheel arch, €1,900.
Third parties: The other driver and their insurer
Evidence:
Signed constat amiable
Flight booking and funeral notice
Photos
What happened (answer): A genuine car park collision with a complete joint report. The late declaration had a good reason and caused the insurer no harm.
Missing information (answer): Confirmation from the other insurer that it has the same constat
Innocent explanations (answer): A bereavement abroad is an obvious reason for delay
Questions to ask (answer): Confirm the car is still unrepaired for the assessor
Next steps (answer):
Do not refuse: under the Code des assurances, a late declaration can only lead to loss of cover if the insurer proves the delay caused it prejudice, and there is none here
Process the claim under the joint report and the inter-insurer agreements
Correct the clerk’s proposal and remind the team of the prejudice requirement
Assessment (answer): Genuine and payable. The delay is explained and harmless; refusing would be unlawful.
Recommended action (answer): Accept the declaration and handle the claim on the constat.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Claim handled normally; other insurer bears the cost under the constat
Team briefed on late declarations
Tags: late declaration, 5 working days, déchéance, prejudice, constat amiable, Code des assurances

Title: Half at fault, charged the full malus
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder and another driver both changed lanes into each other on a ring road in Nantes in the rain. The insurers settled liability 50/50. At renewal, his bonus-malus coefficient went up by 25%, the increase for a fully responsible claim. He complained in writing six weeks ago and has had only an automatic acknowledgment. He has asked how to go to the insurance mediator.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): Your own letter says liability was shared fifty-fifty. My friend who works in insurance says half liability means half the increase. I've written once and heard nothing. I want this corrected and I want to know how to complain properly.
Other accounts:
Liability settlement letter (Document):
Following the inter-insurer agreement, liability for this claim is shared: 50% your responsibility.

Renewal notice (Document):
Bonus-malus coefficient: previous 0.68, new 0.85 (increase of 25% for a responsible claim).
Damage: His Mégane: front-right wing and door, repaired.
Third parties: The other driver and their insurer
Evidence:
Liability settlement letter
Renewal notice
Complaint letter and acknowledgment
What happened (answer): A shared-liability collision rated as if he were fully responsible. The rules give half the increase for partial responsibility.
Missing information (answer): The insurer’s substantive reply to the complaint
Inconsistencies (answer): Liability was settled at 50%; the malus applied was the full 25%
Innocent explanations (answer): Rating systems sometimes apply a full malus by default when liability is entered as "responsible"
Questions to ask (answer): Check how the liability split was entered in the rating system
Next steps (answer):
Correct the coefficient: for a partly responsible claim the increase is 12.5%, not 25%, giving 0.76 after rounding down to two decimals
Refund the premium overcharged and send a substantive written reply
Explain his rights: the insurer should answer complaints within two months, and he can refer the matter to La Médiation de l’Assurance if he remains unhappy
Check for other policyholders affected by the same rating error
Assessment (answer): Disputed on its face but clear on the rules: shared liability carries half the malus. The complaint should be upheld.
Recommended action (answer): Correct the coefficient, refund the difference and reply substantively with his mediation rights.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Coefficient corrected and premium refunded
Rating error found on other shared-liability claims and fixed
Tags: bonus-malus, shared liability, 25%, 12.5%, complaint, Médiation de l’assurance

Title: Torched outside his shop during the unrest
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder's bakkie was set alight by a crowd during violent unrest in Pietermaritzburg while it was parked outside his hardware shop. A claims handler has drafted a rejection under the comprehensive section's exclusion for riot, strike and civil commotion. The policy schedule shows a SASRIA premium charged every month for special risks cover on the vehicle.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): The crowd came down the street throwing things and setting cars alight, I locked myself in the shop. By the time it was safe the bakkie was burnt to the frame. The police came the next day and gave me a case number. I pay for SASRIA every month, it's on my statement.
Other accounts:
SAPS case summary (Report):
Public violence and malicious damage to property during unrest in the area. Several vehicles and shops set alight. Complainant's vehicle burnt while parked. Case registered.

Policy schedule (Document):
Comprehensive motor. Exclusion: riot, strike, civil commotion and public disorder. SASRIA special risks cover: included, premium charged monthly.
Damage: Toyota Hilux burnt out, total loss; retail value about R310,000.
Third parties: Unknown rioters
Evidence:
SAPS case summary
Policy schedule showing SASRIA cover
Photos of the burnt vehicle
What happened (answer): The vehicle was destroyed in public unrest. That is excluded from the comprehensive section but is exactly what the SASRIA cover on his schedule is for.
Missing information (answer): Any news or police reports confirming unrest in that street on that date, if SASRIA asks
Innocent explanations (answer): Handlers who see the riot exclusion may not check the SASRIA section of the schedule
Questions to ask (answer): Confirm the date and street against the reports of unrest
Next steps (answer):
Do not reject: the riot exclusion removes the loss from the comprehensive section, but the SASRIA cover on his schedule responds to riot and public disorder
Submit the claim under the SASRIA cover with the SAPS case number and evidence of the unrest, within the required time limits
Explain the process to him and keep him informed
Correct the draft rejection
Assessment (answer): Genuine and covered under SASRIA. The draft rejection looks only at the comprehensive exclusion.
Recommended action (answer): Process the claim under the SASRIA cover and withdraw the rejection.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Paid under SASRIA as a total loss
Handler guidance updated to check special risks cover
Tags: SASRIA, unrest, riot, public disorder, special risks, SAPS case number

Title: A pothole reported five weeks earlier on the municipal app
Accident type: Single vehicle or loss of control
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder hit a deep, water-filled pothole on a municipal road in Pretoria at night, damaging two rims, two tyres and the front suspension. The claim is R18,400. A resident's report about the same pothole was logged on the municipality's service app five weeks before, with a reference number and a photo. The insurer is paying the claim and is considering recovery from the municipality.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): It was raining and the hole was full of water, it looked like a puddle. The bang was huge and two tyres went flat. A neighbour showed me that people had reported that exact pothole weeks ago and nothing was done.
Other accounts:
Municipal service request (Record or log):
Service request logged five weeks before the incident: "large pothole, danger to vehicles", with a photo and location matching the incident. Status: open, not attended.

Repair quote (Document):
Two alloy rims, two tyres, front left lower control arm and wheel alignment. R18,400.
Damage: Two rims, two tyres, front suspension arm; R18,400.
Third parties: The municipality
Evidence:
Municipal service request with photo
Repair quote
Photos of the pothole at night
What happened (answer): A genuine pothole impact on a defect the municipality had been told about and left unrepaired.
Missing information (answer):
Measurements of the pothole
Whether warning signs were placed
Innocent explanations (answer): A water-filled pothole at night looks like a puddle, so hitting it is not careless driving
Questions to ask (answer): Ask her for daylight photos and measurements of the pothole
Next steps (answer):
Pay her claim under the comprehensive cover, less her excess
Send the municipality written notice of the claim within six months, as the law on legal proceedings against organs of state requires, or the recovery may be lost
Use the service request to show the municipality knew of the danger and did nothing for five weeks
Include her excess in the recovery
Assessment (answer): Genuine, with a good recovery case because the defect had been reported. The six-month notice is the key deadline.
Recommended action (answer): Pay the claim and serve notice on the municipality in time, using the prior report as evidence.

Municipality settles after notice and the service request evidence
Recovery lost because notice was sent after six months
Tags: pothole, municipality, notice within six months, organ of state, recovery, prior report

Title: Hijacked at nine, but the tracker was cut at twenty to
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder reported that his Toyota Hilux was hijacked at gunpoint at 21:00 at a traffic light in Midrand. He opened a SAPS case at 23:30. The tracking company's data shows the vehicle drove to an address in Soshanguve at 20:15, stopped there, and the tracking unit raised a tamper alert at 20:40 before going offline. The Soshanguve address is registered to his brother-in-law.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): Two men with a gun came to my window at the robot and told me to get out. They drove off with the bakkie. I was so shocked I sat on the pavement for an hour before I went to the police. I don't know anything about Soshanguve, maybe the tracker is wrong.
Other accounts:
Tracking company data (Record or log):
19:55 departed the policyholder's home. 20:15 arrived at an address in Soshanguve; ignition off. 20:40 tamper alert: unit power disconnected. No further signal. No movement recorded towards Midrand.

SAPS case summary (Report):
Complainant reports a hijacking at about 21:00 at an intersection in Midrand. Case opened at 23:30. No witnesses recorded. Intersection camera footage requested.
Damage: Toyota Hilux reported hijacked; value about R480,000.
Third parties:
The brother-in-law
Tracking company
Evidence:
Tracking data
SAPS case summary
What happened (answer): The bakkie was driven to his brother-in-law's address and the tracker was disconnected there before the time of the reported hijacking.
Missing information (answer):
Intersection camera footage in Midrand
His phone location data for the evening
Inconsistencies (answer): He says the bakkie was taken in Midrand at 21:00; the tracker shows it at a Soshanguve address with the unit disconnected at 20:40
Fraud indicators (answer):
Tracker disconnected at a relative’s address before the reported hijacking
Two-and-a-half hour delay before the police report
He denies knowing the address
Innocent explanations (answer): Tracking units can misreport after tampering, but the tamper alert itself came before the reported time
Questions to ask (answer):
Ask him to account for the vehicle’s journey to Soshanguve
Ask the brother-in-law whether the bakkie was at his house
Next steps (answer):
Interview him with the tracking data, in line with the policy’s claims conditions
Get the Midrand intersection footage through SAPS
Do not settle while the tracking data is unexplained
If the data stands, reject the claim and report the false statement to SAPS
Assessment (answer): Potential fraud with strong data: the vehicle and tracker were at a relative's address before the reported hijacking.
Recommended action (answer): Investigate with the tracking evidence and footage before any decision.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Bakkie found at a scrapyard linked to the brother-in-law; claim rejected
Claim withdrawn after the interview
Tags: hijacking, tracking device, tamper alert, false theft, relative’s address, SAPS

Title: Rejected for no tracker, a condition nobody mentioned on the phone
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder's Toyota Fortuner was stolen from a shopping centre parking lot in Johannesburg. Eighteen-minute call. Questions on vehicle, overnight parking, driver history. No mention of a tracking device requirement. Agent says: "You're fully comprehensive, you're covered for theft and hijacking."

Policy schedule endorsement (Document):
Theft and hijacking cover for this vehicle is conditional on an approved tracking device being fitted and active. Documents emailed the day after the sale.
Damage: Toyota Fortuner stolen; value about R560,000; finance outstanding.
Third parties: The finance house
Evidence:
Call recording
Policy schedule endorsement
SAPS case number
Shopping centre CCTV
What happened (answer): A genuine theft. The tracking condition is in the documents but was not disclosed in the sale, and the agent described the cover as complete.
Missing information (answer):
Whether he read the emailed documents
Whether a tracker would likely have led to recovery
Inconsistencies (answer): The agent said he was covered for theft; the documents make theft cover conditional on a tracker
Innocent explanations (answer): Customers buying by phone rely on what the agent says
Questions to ask (answer): Ask whether he received and read the emailed schedule
Next steps (answer):
Review the rejection under the treating customers fairly principles and the Policyholder Protection Rules: a material condition that was not disclosed at sale, with the agent stating full theft cover, is unlikely to be upheld by the ombud
Consider paying the claim, or at least a fair settlement, rather than relying on the endorsement
Respond to his complaint in writing with reasons and explain his right to approach the ombud
Fix the sales script so material conditions are disclosed on the call
Assessment (answer): Disputed, but the sales failure weighs heavily against the insurer. Relying on an undisclosed condition is likely to be found unfair.
Recommended action (answer): Reconsider the rejection, likely pay, and fix the sales disclosure.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Claim paid after internal review; sales script changed
Ombud recommends payment in full
