Title: A side-swipe in Johor Bahru, and two versions at the merge
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder drove his Singapore-registered car to Johor Bahru for the weekend. Where two lanes merge after a traffic light, his car and a Malaysian car side-swiped each other. Both drivers made police reports in Johor within 24 hours, each blaming the other. The Malaysian driver has claimed against the policyholder's Singapore insurer for repairs and three weeks of car rental. The policyholder reported the accident to his insurer the next morning.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): My lane was the one that continued, his lane ended with arrows to merge. He tried to squeeze in at the last moment and hit my front door. I made the police report at the station near the checkpoint before driving back. I have a front dashcam.
Other accounts:
Malaysian driver’s police report (translated summary) (Report):
Complainant states the Singapore car moved left into his lane while merging and hit his car. Complainant's car damaged on the right side.

Policyholder’s dashcam summary (Record or log):
Front camera: the policyholder's lane continues; arrows painted in the left lane indicate it ends. The Malaysian car comes alongside from the ending lane and moves right; contact at the policyholder's front-left door. The policyholder's car stays within its lane markings.
Damage: Policyholder's Mazda 3: front-left door and wing. Malaysian car: right-side doors.
Third parties: The Malaysian driver and his insurer
Evidence:
Both police reports
Dashcam footage
Photos of the merge markings
What happened (answer): The Malaysian driver merged from an ending lane into the policyholder's continuing lane. The dashcam supports the policyholder.
Missing information (answer):
The Malaysian car's own insurer and any dashcam
Rental invoices
Inconsistencies (answer): Each driver says the other moved into their lane
Innocent explanations (answer): Unfamiliar road markings across the border cause genuine misunderstandings
Questions to ask (answer): Ask the Malaysian driver’s side for any footage and the rental invoices
Next steps (answer):
Confirm the policy’s geographical area covers West Malaysia, and that both reports were made in time
Deny the third-party claim on the dashcam evidence, or negotiate a split if the other side produces contrary footage
Handle the policyholder’s own damage under his cover and pursue the Malaysian driver’s insurer for recovery
Use a Malaysian adjuster for the third-party side if needed
Assessment (answer): Disputed, but the dashcam and the lane markings favour the policyholder. The Malaysian driver merged from the ending lane.
Recommended action (answer): Defend the third-party claim on the footage and recover the policyholder's losses.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Malaysian insurer accepts liability after viewing the footage
Settled 70/30 in the policyholder’s favour
Tags: Malaysia, cross-border, West Malaysia cover, Malaysian police report, lane merge, third-party claim

Title: Rear-ended by his friend, with a dent from three months ago
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder Daniel Koh reported that he rear-ended his friend Jason Lim's car at low speed in a Jurong car park. Both reported the accident under the Motor Claims Framework and Mr Lim has claimed S$6,900 against Mr Koh's policy. The damage includes a rust-pitted dent in the bumper and a tail lamp with dirt inside its crack. The workshop is run by Mr Koh's cousin. A photo on Mr Lim's social media from three months earlier shows the same dent.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): (Daniel Koh, our policyholder) I was slow, maybe 10 km/h, and I tapped Jason's car when he stopped suddenly. We're friends so we went to my cousin's workshop, he gives good prices. I told him to claim from my insurance since it was my fault.
Other accounts:
Insurer’s assessor (Report):
Fresh contact marks on the bumper corner consistent with a low-speed tap. Separate dent with rust pitting in the paint, older than the incident. Tail lamp crack contains dirt and moisture. Estimated fresh damage S$1,300.

Social media photo (Record or log):
Photo posted by Mr Lim three months before the incident, showing his car at a car meet. The dent on the rear bumper is visible in the same position.
Damage: Fresh contact marks on the bumper corner. Older dent and cracked tail lamp included in the S$6,900 claim.
Third parties:
Jason Lim, the claimant
Policyholder's cousin's workshop
Evidence:
Assessor's report
Social media photo
Workshop estimate
Both accident reports
What happened (answer): A real low-speed tap between friends, used to put older damage on the policyholder's insurance.
Missing information (answer):
Car park CCTV
The workshop's photos before repair
Inconsistencies (answer): The claim includes a dent visible in a photo taken three months before the incident
Fraud indicators (answer):
Claim between friends repaired at a relative’s workshop
Old damage included in the estimate
Claim far above the fresh damage
Innocent explanations (answer): Friends often use a familiar workshop, and the workshop may have quoted everything it saw
Questions to ask (answer):
Ask Mr Lim to explain the dent in the earlier photo
Ask the car park for CCTV
Next steps (answer):
Offer to pay the fresh damage only, about S$1,300, and decline the older items with the photo as the reason
Put the photo to both men in interviews
Refer to the fraud team if they persist with the full amount
Note the link between the policyholder and the workshop
Assessment (answer): Potential fraud: a genuine minor tap with older damage added, arranged between friends and a related workshop.
Recommended action (answer): Pay only the fresh damage and investigate if the full claim is pressed.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Claim reduced to S$1,300 and accepted
Referred after the claimant insists on the full amount
Tags: collusion, friends, old damage, social media photo, workshop link, Motor Claims Framework

Title: "I was driving," until the workshop camera showed her son
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder reported that she hit a bollard while parking at a condominium in Tampines. Her policy has a S$600 excess, plus additional excesses of S$2,500 each for a young driver and an inexperienced driver. The car's own camera and the condominium's CCTV show her 22-year-old son, who passed his test a year ago, driving. When shown the footage she admitted it and apologized.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): I panicked. My son is careful, he just misjudged the bollard. I knew there was a big excess for young drivers and I thought it was a small accident, it wouldn't matter who drove. I'm sorry, I should have told the truth.
Other accounts:
Condominium CCTV summary (Record or log):
A young man drives the car into the bay and strikes the bollard. He gets out from the driver's seat. The policyholder arrives ten minutes later.

Policy schedule (Document):
Excess: S$600. Additional excess S$2,500 where the driver is under 27, and S$2,500 where the driver has held a licence for less than 2 years. Named drivers: policyholder only. Unnamed drivers permitted with the additional excesses.
Damage: Toyota Corolla Altis: front bumper and grille, S$2,900.
Third parties: None
Evidence:
Condominium CCTV
Car's camera
Policy schedule
Her admission
What happened (answer): A genuine bollard strike by her son. She named herself as the driver to avoid S$5,000 of additional excesses, then admitted it.
Missing information (answer): The son's own account of the incident
Inconsistencies (answer): Her report named herself; the footage shows her son driving
Fraud indicators (answer): False statement about the driver to reduce the excess
Innocent explanations (answer): A parent protecting a child in a moment of panic, corrected before payment
Questions to ask (answer): Confirm the son’s licence date
Next steps (answer):
Apply the correct excesses for the actual driver: S$600 plus both additional excesses; with damage of S$2,900, the excesses exceed the loss, so nothing is payable
Record the false statement and treat it seriously: a deliberate misstatement in a claim can justify refusing the claim and may affect future cover
Warn her in writing, as the statement was corrected before any payment
Offer to add her son as a named driver at the correct premium
Assessment (answer): Suspicious conduct on a genuine incident: a deliberate but corrected misstatement. Applying the correct excesses resolves the claim.
Recommended action (answer): Apply the correct excesses, record and warn about the false statement, and update the named drivers.
Possible outcomes (answer):
No payment due after excesses; warning issued
Insurer declines to renew after a second misstatement
Tags: additional excess, young driver, inexperienced driver, unnamed driver, false statement, correction

Title: A delivery rider’s S$85,000 claim and the online assessment tool
Fraud type: False hire, towing or storage costs
Claim notification (exhibit A): Our policyholder turned right across a delivery rider at a junction in Tampines. The rider fractured his wrist. His lawyers claim S$85,000, including six months of lost earnings. The court's online assessment tool, using past cases, suggests a range for the wrist injury well below that and a liability split favouring the rider. The delivery platform's records show he resumed deliveries three weeks after the accident.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): (Through his lawyers) Our client could not work for six months and still has pain gripping the handlebars. He supports his parents. The insurer's driver turned without looking.
Other accounts:
Online assessment tool result (Report):
Liability: right-turning car mainly at fault; rider may bear a small share for speed. Quantum for a wrist fracture with good recovery: a range far below the amount claimed. Loss of earnings to be proved by records.

Delivery platform records (Record or log):
Account inactive for 21 days after the accident date. Deliveries resumed thereafter at about 80% of previous weekly volume, returning to normal within two months.
Damage: Fractured wrist treated with a cast; physiotherapy. Motorcycle repaired.
Third parties:
Muhammad Faizal
His lawyers
Evidence:
Online assessment result
Delivery platform records
Medical report
Police report
What happened (answer): A genuine injury mainly caused by our policyholder. The claimed earnings loss is overstated: he returned to work after three weeks.
Missing information (answer): A specialist report on any lasting grip weakness
Inconsistencies (answer): Six months of lost earnings claimed; platform records show work resumed after three weeks
Fraud indicators (answer): Earnings claim contradicted by platform records
Innocent explanations (answer): He may have worked in pain at reduced volume, which is a real loss for a shorter period
Questions to ask (answer): Ask for his earnings before and after the accident from the platform
Next steps (answer):
Accept that liability rests mainly on the policyholder
Value the injury using the online assessment range and the medical evidence
Pay lost earnings for the three weeks off and the reduced volume afterwards, on the platform records
Make a reasoned offer and use the tool’s range in negotiation or mediation
Assessment (answer): Genuine injury, overstated claim. The assessment tool and the platform records set a fair range well below the demand.
Recommended action (answer): Offer within the tool's range with proven earnings losses.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Settled at S$31,000
Resolved at court-assisted mediation within the tool’s range
Tags: Motor Accident Claims Online, MACO, quantum, liability apportionment, loss of earnings, delivery platform records

Title: Assessed at €12,000 by the Injuries Resolution Board, and a handler who wants to reject it
Claim notification (exhibit A): Our policyholder rear-ended Ms Byrne's car in Galway. She suffered a neck injury and a wrist sprain. The Injuries Resolution Board assessed her claim at €12,000 under the Personal Injuries Guidelines, supported by a medical report. The handler wants to reject the assessment because "whiplash is overpaid". If the insurer rejects it, the Board will issue an authorisation and she can sue.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): (Through her solicitor) Our client has accepted the assessment. She has had physiotherapy for five months and still has symptoms in her wrist. If your client rejects it we will issue proceedings.
Other accounts:
Medical report summary (Report):
Neck soft-tissue injury, substantial recovery within six months. Wrist sprain with persisting symptoms at five months, prognosis for recovery within twelve months. No pre-existing problems.

Injuries Resolution Board assessment (Document):
General damages assessed under the Personal Injuries Guidelines for the dominant wrist injury with an uplift for the neck injury, plus special damages. Total €12,000. Claimant has accepted.
Damage: Neck soft-tissue injury and wrist sprain. Car damage settled separately.
Third parties:
Aoife Byrne
Her solicitor
Evidence:
Medical report
Board assessment
Physiotherapy invoices
What happened (answer): A genuine injury fairly assessed under the Guidelines. Rejecting it would mean litigation with higher costs and little prospect of a lower award.
Missing information (answer): Any medical evidence the handler relies on for a lower figure
Innocent explanations (answer): Handlers sometimes judge awards by pre-Guidelines experience
Questions to ask (answer): Ask the handler what in the medical evidence supports a lower figure
Next steps (answer):
Check the assessment against the Guidelines brackets for the dominant injury and the medical prognosis
Accept within the time allowed if, as it appears, the assessment is within the Guidelines
Explain to the business that rejection leads to an authorisation, court proceedings and legal costs that will likely exceed any saving
Reject only with specific medical or factual grounds, recorded on file
Assessment (answer): Genuine and fairly assessed. Accepting the assessment is the sensible and fair outcome.
Recommended action (answer): Accept the €12,000 assessment within the time allowed.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Assessment accepted and paid
Rejected, then settled in court at €13,500 plus costs
Tags: Injuries Resolution Board, Personal Injuries Guidelines, assessment, authorisation, litigation costs, acceptance

Title: Rear-ended in Christchurch, and she wants him to pay for her neck
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder was rear-ended at lights in Christchurch. She has a neck injury and two weeks off work. She has asked her insurer to claim compensation for her injury and lost wages from the other driver, along with the repairs to her car. The other driver admitted fault and is insured.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): He was on his phone, he admitted it. My neck still hurts and I lost two weeks' pay. In Australia my cousin got money from the other driver's insurance for her injuries. Why can't I?
Other accounts:
Other driver (Statement):
I looked down at my phone and went into the back of her car. My fault completely. My insurer's details are attached.

GP note (Report):
Neck sprain. Two weeks off work. ACC claim lodged by the GP on the day of the consultation.
Damage: Her Corolla: rear bumper and boot, NZ$3,200. Neck sprain, two weeks off work.
Third parties:
The other driver and his insurer
ACC
Evidence:
Other driver's admission
GP note with the ACC claim
Repair quote
What happened (answer): A genuine not-at-fault collision. Her injury is covered by ACC, which bars suing for personal injury compensation; her car damage is claimed from the other driver's insurer.
Missing information (answer): ACC’s decision on weekly compensation
Innocent explanations (answer): Rules in Australia are different, which is a common source of confusion
Questions to ask (answer): Ask whether ACC has confirmed her weekly compensation
Next steps (answer):
Explain that ACC covers her injury, treatment and lost earnings on a no-fault basis, and that New Zealand law bars suing for compensation for a personal injury covered by ACC
Claim her car repairs and excess from the other driver’s insurer, or pay under her own policy and recover
Help her follow up the ACC weekly compensation
Assessment (answer): Genuine and not at fault. The injury goes through ACC; the property damage goes against the other driver's insurer.

ACC pays weekly compensation; car repaired and recovered
She accepts the explanation after a call

Title: A pedestrian in Osaka, and the compulsory cover’s ¥1.2 million ceiling
Claim notification (exhibit A): Our policyholder struck a 70-year-old pedestrian, Mr Sato, at a crossing in Osaka in the rain. He suffered a fractured hip and has been in hospital for six weeks. Medical costs so far are ¥3.4 million. The policyholder has both the compulsory automobile liability insurance and our voluntary insurance. The family has asked who will pay the hospital and whether they need a lawyer.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): (Mr Sato's daughter) My father was on the crossing with the green light. The hospital is asking us for payment. He may need care at home after this. We don't know which insurance pays what.
Other accounts:
Police report extract (Report):
Pedestrian struck on a crossing while the pedestrian signal was green. Driver states rain on the windscreen reduced visibility. Driver at fault.

Hospital statement (Record or log):
Hip fracture, surgery and six weeks of inpatient care. Costs to date ¥3,400,000. Rehabilitation expected for several months.
Damage: Fractured hip, surgery, long rehabilitation.
Third parties:
Kenji Sato and his family
The hospital
The compulsory insurance insurer
Evidence:
Police report
Hospital statement
Both policies
What happened (answer): A serious pedestrian injury caused by our policyholder. The costs already exceed the compulsory insurance limit for injury, so the voluntary insurance must cover the rest.
Missing information (answer): A prognosis for long-term care needs
Innocent explanations (answer): Rain on the windscreen at a crossing explains, but does not excuse, the driver not seeing him
Questions to ask (answer): Ask the family about his care needs after discharge
Next steps (answer):
Offer one-stop handling: the voluntary insurer deals with the family and the hospital for the whole claim and recovers the compulsory portion from the compulsory insurer
Pay the hospital directly so the family is not asked for payment
Explain that the compulsory cover pays injury losses up to ¥1.2 million and the voluntary insurance pays above that
Assess consolation money and future care fairly, and tell the family they may consult a lawyer
Assessment (answer): Genuine and serious; the policyholder is at fault. The voluntary insurance carries most of the cost above the compulsory limit.
Recommended action (answer): Take on one-stop handling, pay the hospital directly, and plan for care costs.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Settled after rehabilitation including home care costs
Family instructs a lawyer; settled at court standards
Tags: compulsory automobile liability insurance, CALI, voluntary insurance, one-stop handling, consolation money, pedestrian

Title: A friendly report signed by both drivers, and no offer after six weeks
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder was not at fault in a junction collision in Milan and claimed under the direct compensation system, which means her own insurer handles the claim. She submitted a joint accident report (CAI) signed by both drivers on 2 March, with photos and a repair estimate. On 15 April she had received no offer and no reasons. She has complained to the insurer and says she will go to the regulator.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): The other driver signed that it was his fault. I sent everything the same day. I've had no offer, no refusal, nothing. I've read that there are deadlines. My car has been parked for six weeks.
Other accounts:
Joint accident report (CAI) (Document):
Signed by both drivers on 2 March. Vehicle B failed to give way at a junction and struck vehicle A. Vehicle B driver accepts responsibility.

Claim log (Record or log):
Claim received with the signed CAI, photos and estimate on 2 March. Inspection done 10 March. No offer or reasoned refusal issued. Complaint received 15 April.
Damage: Her Fiat 500: front-right wing and bumper, estimate €2,300.
Third parties: The other driver and his insurer
Evidence:
Signed CAI
Claim log
Photos and estimate
What happened (answer): A straightforward not-at-fault claim with a CAI signed by both drivers, left without an offer past the statutory period.
Missing information (answer): Any reason recorded for the delay
Innocent explanations (answer): Inspection backlogs after holidays can delay offers, but do not extend the legal period
Questions to ask (answer): Check whether other direct compensation claims are overdue
Next steps (answer):
Make the offer now: under article 148 of the Code, the insurer must make a reasoned offer or refusal within 30 days where the CAI is signed by both drivers (60 days otherwise, 90 for injuries)
Pay interest for the delay and answer her complaint within the regulator’s time limit
Tell her she can complain to IVASS if she is not satisfied
Fix the cause of the delay
Assessment (answer): Genuine and overdue. The 30-day period for a jointly signed report has long passed.
Recommended action (answer): Make the offer with interest, answer the complaint, and explain the IVASS route.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Offer accepted within a week of the complaint
IVASS complaint leads to a sanction for repeated delays
Tags: direct compensation, CAI, Codice delle assicurazioni private, article 148, 30 days, IVASS complaint

Title: A fourteen-year-old Ibiza worth €1,800 and a repair bill of €4,200
Claim notification (exhibit A): Our policyholder hit the side of Ms Ruiz's 14-year-old Seat Ibiza in Valencia. Liability is accepted. The repair estimate is €4,200. The car's market value (valor venal) is about €1,800. She insists on repair, saying the car is in excellent condition, has low mileage and she cannot find a replacement for that money. The handler has offered €1,800.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): I've looked after that car for fourteen years and it has 90,000 km. For €1,800 I'd get a wreck. I use it every day to take my mother to the hospital. It was his fault, why should I lose my car?
Other accounts:
Valuation (Report):
Market value of a comparable Seat Ibiza of this age: about €1,800. Vehicle in above-average condition, 90,000 km, full service history.

Repair estimate (Document):
Two doors, B-pillar repair and paint: €4,200.
Damage: Seat Ibiza: two doors and B-pillar.
Third parties: Carmen Ruiz
Evidence:
Valuation
Repair estimate
Service history
What happened (answer): A genuine claim where repair costs more than twice the market value. Spanish practice usually pays market value plus an uplift for the owner's loss when repair is disproportionate, but the gap and the car's condition are argued.
Missing information (answer): Quotes for comparable cars in similar condition
Innocent explanations (answer): Owners of well-kept older cars face real replacement difficulty
Questions to ask (answer): Ask her for listings of comparable cars in similar condition
Next steps (answer):
Do not stop at the bare market value: offer the market value plus an uplift for the owner’s loss (valor de afección), as Spanish practice commonly allows where repair is disproportionate
Consider whether the repair is truly disproportionate given the car’s condition and her daily need; courts may allow repair where the cost is not excessive in context
Make a reasoned offer explaining the basis, and keep the option of paying for repair if the difference is modest
Assessment (answer): Genuine, with a real dispute about measure. €1,800 alone undercompensates her; a reasoned uplift or a negotiated repair is fairer.
Recommended action (answer): Offer market value plus an afección uplift with reasons, and consider repair if the gap narrows.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Settled at €2,700 including the uplift
Agreed to pay for repair after she finds no comparable car
Tags: valor venal, valor de afección, repair versus value, disproportionate repair, third-party settlement, Spain

Title: Rear-ended on the Federal Highway, and his no-claim discount on the line
Claim notification (exhibit A): Policyholder was rear-ended in heavy rain on the Federal Highway in Kuala Lumpur. To get his car repaired quickly he claimed under his own policy through the knock-for-knock arrangement, which protects his no-claim discount when he is not at fault. The other driver's insurer now disputes liability, saying the policyholder braked suddenly for no reason. The policyholder's dashcam shows a motorcycle cutting in front of him.
Claimant's statement (exhibit B): A motorcycle cut across in front of me in the rain and I had to brake. The car behind was too close. I made the police report the same evening. I chose the knock-for-knock claim so I wouldn't lose my 55% discount.
Other accounts:
Dashcam summary (Record or log):
Motorcycle cuts across from the left lane without signalling about 15 metres ahead. Policyholder brakes firmly; the car stops. About 1.5 seconds later the rear impact occurs.

Other insurer’s letter (Document):
Our insured states your insured braked suddenly and without reason. We do not accept liability under the knock-for-knock arrangement.
Damage: His Honda City: rear bumper, boot and tail lamps, RM 5,600.
Third parties:
The other driver and his insurer
The unidentified motorcyclist
Evidence:
Dashcam footage
Police reports
Repair invoice
What happened (answer): A rear-end collision after the policyholder braked for a motorcyclist. A following driver should keep a safe distance, so liability rests mainly with the other driver.
Missing information (answer): The other driver's police report
Inconsistencies (answer): The other driver says he braked for no reason; the dashcam shows a motorcycle cutting in
Innocent explanations (answer): From behind, a driver may not see why the car in front braked
Questions to ask (answer): Ask for the other driver's police report
Next steps (answer):
Repair the car under the knock-for-knock claim and keep his no-claim discount protected while liability is resolved
Send the dashcam footage to the other insurer: braking for a hazard does not shift fault from a driver who failed to keep a safe distance
Pursue recovery under the knock-for-knock arrangement and escalate through the industry dispute process if refused
Assessment (answer): Disputed only on a weak point. The footage shows a real hazard, and the following driver was too close.
Recommended action (answer): Protect his discount, share the footage, and recover from the other insurer.
Possible outcomes (answer):
Other insurer accepts after viewing the footage; discount protected
Resolved through the industry dispute process in his favour
Tags: knock-for-knock, OD-KfK, no-claim discount, recovery, police report, sudden braking
